name: Hair Fall
summary: Excessive daily shedding, a widening parting or a thinning ponytail — assessed for the underlying cause rather than treated on the scalp alone.
intro: Losing 50–100 hairs a day is normal. Persistent shedding beyond that, or hair that no longer grows back at the same density, usually points to something systemic — nutrition, thyroid function, hormones, illness, stress or post-partum change. Homeopathic treatment at the clinic begins by identifying which of these applies to you, because scalp-only treatment rarely holds if the cause sits elsewhere.

A parting that has visibly widened over months
Reduced ponytail thickness
Hair that breaks mid-shaft rather than falling from the root
Scalp becoming visible under direct light
Slow regrowth after a shedding episode
causes: Iron, vitamin D, vitamin B12 or protein deficiency
Thyroid dysfunction (hypo- or hyperthyroidism)
Hormonal shifts — PCOD, post-partum, perimenopause
Telogen effluvium following fever, surgery, illness or acute stress
Genetic predisposition to androgenetic pattern loss
Chronic scalp inflammation or untreated dandruff
Certain medications and crash dieting
treatment: A detailed first consultation covering medical history, family history, diet, sleep, stress and menstrual history
Review of existing blood reports; referral for thyroid, ferritin, vitamin D or hormonal testing where indicated
Scalp and hair-shaft examination, in person or via clear photographs for online consultations
An individualised homeopathic prescription — selected for your constitution and cause, not a fixed protocol
Nutritional and hair-care guidance, including what to stop doing
Scheduled follow-ups to reassess and adjust the prescription

expectedResults.detail: The focus is on identifying and addressing the underlying cause. Shedding often continues during this period — this is expected and not a sign of failure.
Many patients report that daily shedding begins to settle. Fine regrowth may appear along the hairline and parting.
Where regrowth occurs, this is when it becomes visible in density. Progress is reviewed at each follow-up with comparison photographs.
Response varies considerably between individuals depending on cause, duration and adherence. Some conditions require long-term management rather than a fixed course.

faqs.question: How soon will I see a difference?
faqs.answer: This varies genuinely from person to person. Hair grows roughly one centimetre a month, so any treatment needs time before visible change is possible. Most patients are asked to allow three to four months before assessing progress, with follow-ups along the way.

faqs.question: Do I need blood tests before starting?
faqs.answer: Not always, but often. If your history suggests thyroid, iron or hormonal involvement, Dr. Riji will ask for specific tests. If you already have recent reports, bring or upload them — it saves both time and cost.

faqs.question: Will the hair fall return if I stop treatment?
faqs.answer: It depends entirely on the cause. Shedding triggered by a one-off event such as illness or childbirth usually settles and stays settled. Hair fall driven by an ongoing condition — thyroid disease or PCOD, for instance — needs that condition managed continuously.

faqs.question: Can homeopathy be taken alongside my other medicines?
faqs.answer: In most cases yes, but you must disclose everything you are taking, including supplements and topical treatments. Never stop a prescribed conventional medication without speaking to the doctor who prescribed it.

intro: Alopecia areata appears as smooth, round patches of hair loss that develop over days or weeks. It is an autoimmune condition — the body's own immune response targets the hair follicle. The follicle is usually not destroyed, which is why regrowth is possible. Because it is systemic rather than local, treatment addresses the immune picture and the person as a whole.

Loss in the beard, eyebrows or eyelashes

Genetic predisposition — a family history of autoimmune conditions is common
Significant emotional or physical stress as a trigger
Associated thyroid disease, vitiligo or other autoimmune conditions
Recent viral illness in some presentations
treatment: Careful history-taking covering onset, triggers, family autoimmune history and emotional context
Examination of patch borders to assess whether the condition is active or stabilising
Screening for associated thyroid and autoimmune involvement where indicated
Constitutional homeopathic prescribing aimed at the immune picture rather than the patch alone
Support for stress and sleep, which frequently influence the course
Regular photographic review to track patch borders objectively

expectedResults.detail: The first goal is stabilisation — stopping new patches from forming. Existing patches may not change during this window.
Fine, colourless vellus hair often appears within patches first. This is an encouraging sign and typically precedes pigmented regrowth.
Where the response is good, vellus hair thickens and regains pigment. Extensive or long-standing cases progress more slowly.
Alopecia areata can relapse even after complete regrowth, and some cases do not respond. This is discussed openly at the first consultation rather than after treatment begins.

faqs.question: Is alopecia areata permanent?
faqs.answer: Usually not. The follicles are typically dormant rather than destroyed, which is why regrowth is possible even after months. However, the condition is unpredictable — it can resolve, recur, or in a minority of cases progress. Nobody can reliably predict which course an individual will take.

faqs.question: Is it caused by stress?
faqs.answer: Stress is frequently a trigger rather than the root cause. The underlying mechanism is autoimmune. That said, managing stress genuinely matters, because it influences both the course and the likelihood of relapse.

faqs.question: Is it contagious?
faqs.answer: No. Alopecia areata cannot be passed to anyone else by any form of contact.

faqs.question: My child has a patch — is treatment different?
faqs.answer: The approach is the same in principle but the prescription, dosage and consultation style are adapted for children. Paediatric cases are common and are handled gently, with the child's comfort prioritised.

faqs.question: Why does my dandruff keep coming back after shampoo works?
faqs.answer: Medicated shampoos reduce yeast on the scalp surface, which is why they work quickly — and why the problem returns once you stop. They do not change the underlying tendency toward inflammation and sebum production. Treatment aims at that tendency, which is why it takes longer but tends to hold better.

faqs.question: Does dandruff actually cause hair fall?
faqs.answer: Not directly, but the connection is real. Sustained inflammation and repeated scratching weaken the follicle and increase shedding. Treating the scalp often reduces hair fall as a consequence.

faqs.question: Should I stop oiling my hair?
faqs.answer: Not necessarily — but heavy oiling left on an already oily, yeast-affected scalp usually makes things worse. Dr. Riji will advise based on your scalp type rather than applying a blanket rule.

faqs.question: Can grey hair turn black again?
faqs.answer: Honestly, usually not. Where greying is caused by a correctable deficiency such as B12, some pigment recovery is occasionally seen. Where it is genetic, it is not reversible. The realistic and worthwhile goal is slowing further greying.

faqs.question: Is it worth getting tested?
faqs.answer: If greying started before 25, yes. B12 deficiency, thyroid disease and anaemia are all common, all easily tested and all worth correcting for reasons well beyond hair colour.

faqs.question: Does plucking grey hairs make more grow?
faqs.answer: No — that is a myth. Only one hair grows from each follicle. Plucking does damage the follicle over time, though, so it is still best avoided.

faqs.question: My father is bald — will I definitely lose my hair?
faqs.answer: Not definitely. Genetics from both sides of the family influence risk, but onset age and speed vary widely, and factors within your control — scalp health, nutrition, sleep, smoking — influence how fast it progresses.

faqs.question: Do helmets or caps cause this?
faqs.answer: No. Pattern loss is hormonal and genetic. Headwear does not cause it, though very tight or constantly rubbing headwear can add frictional damage on top.

faqs.question: Will I go bald like men do?
faqs.answer: Almost never. Female pattern loss thins the parting and crown but rarely progresses to baldness. The realistic concern is progressive density loss, which is worth addressing early.

faqs.question: Which tests should I do first?

faqs.question: Can hairstyle changes help?
faqs.answer: Styling can disguise thinning but tight styles worsen it. Avoiding traction and harsh chemical processing protects what you have while treatment addresses the cause.

intro: Acute telogen effluvium is the scalp's delayed response to a systemic shock. A fever, operation, delivery, crash diet or intensely stressful period pushes a large share of follicles into their resting phase together; two to three months later those hairs shed in unison, often alarmingly. Understanding the delay matters: the shedding you notice today reflects an event months ago, and in most cases the condition resolves on its own once the trigger has passed.

faqs.question: Will my hair grow back?
faqs.answer: In acute telogen effluvium, almost always yes. The follicles are resting, not damaged. Density typically recovers over six to nine months once the trigger has passed.

faqs.question: Why did this start when my life was calm?
faqs.answer: Because of the built-in delay. Follicles pushed into rest by an event shed their hairs two to three months later — count back and the trigger usually reveals itself.

faqs.question: Should I take supplements to speed it up?
faqs.answer: Only what testing shows you actually need. Correcting a genuine iron or vitamin D deficiency helps recovery; random high-dose supplements do not, and high-dose biotin interferes with thyroid blood tests.

The reassuring feature: it rarely causes visible baldness, because follicles keep cycling rather than miniaturising. The work is in finding and correcting the sustaining factors.

Thyroid dysfunction

Nutritional insufficiency, including low protein intake
Sometimes no single identifiable cause
treatment: Systematic exclusion of sustaining factors — ferritin, thyroid, vitamin D, diet, medication review
Objective baseline photographs, because fluctuation makes memory unreliable
An individualised homeopathic prescription selected for your constitution and the whole clinical picture
Practical hair-care and lifestyle guidance specific to the condition
Follow-up every four to six weeks with standardised comparison photographs

expectedResults.detail: Sustaining factors are hunted down and corrected. Objective photographic baselines are set.
Shedding episodes usually become shorter and less intense.
The condition fluctuates by nature; management aims at longer, more stable good phases, and comparison photographs keep progress honest.

faqs.question: Why can't anyone find the cause?
faqs.answer: Sometimes several small factors sustain it together — borderline ferritin, disturbed sleep, stress — rather than one large one. Methodically correcting each is more productive than searching for a single culprit.

faqs.question: Will I go bald?
faqs.answer: Chronic telogen effluvium very rarely leads to visible baldness. Follicles continue to cycle; density fluctuates but the follicle population is preserved.

faqs.question: How is this different from female pattern loss?
faqs.answer: Pattern loss progressively miniaturises follicles along the parting; chronic effluvium sheds diffusely without miniaturisation. They can co-exist, which is why examination matters.

name: Anagen Effluvium
summary: Rapid hair loss beginning within days to weeks of chemotherapy, radiation or certain toxins — managed supportively, in coordination with your treating specialists.
intro: Anagen effluvium is loss of actively growing hairs, most commonly during chemotherapy or radiotherapy, occasionally from toxin exposure. Because around ninety per cent of scalp hair is in its growth phase at any time, loss is fast and extensive. Two things are said plainly here: this condition is managed alongside — never instead of — your oncology team, and in most cases hair regrows once the causative treatment ends, sometimes with temporary changes in texture or colour.

Rapid, extensive loss affecting most of the scalp
Broken, tapered hair shafts rather than shed bulbs
May involve brows, lashes and body hair
Regrowth usually begins within months of the cause ending

Radiotherapy to the scalp
Certain toxins and heavy metals
Rarely, severe protein-calorie malnutrition
treatment: Coordination with your oncologist or treating physician — their treatment always takes precedence
Gentle scalp care guidance during the loss phase
Supportive homeopathic care for general wellbeing during and after treatment
Nutritional support for regrowth once the causative treatment has finished
Follow-up as regrowth establishes

expectedResults.detail: The focus is comfort, gentle scalp care and general wellbeing. Hair loss during chemotherapy cannot usually be prevented.
Regrowth typically begins within one to three months of the causative treatment ending, sometimes with different texture or colour at first.
Density rebuilds progressively; texture usually normalises over subsequent cycles.

faqs.question: Will my hair come back after chemotherapy?
faqs.answer: In the great majority of cases, yes — regrowth usually starts within one to three months of finishing treatment. Early regrowth may be curlier, finer or differently coloured, and typically normalises over time.

faqs.question: Can homeopathy prevent chemotherapy hair loss?
faqs.answer: No treatment at this clinic prevents it, and you should be cautious of anyone claiming otherwise. Our role is supportive care, and everything is coordinated with your oncology team.

faqs.question: Is this the same as ordinary hair fall?
faqs.answer: No. Ordinary shedding releases resting hairs with a root bulb; anagen effluvium breaks actively growing hairs, which is why onset is so much faster.

name: Alopecia Totalis
summary: Autoimmune loss of all scalp hair — a severe form of alopecia areata, approached with realistic expectations and long-term constitutional care.
intro: Alopecia totalis is the loss of all scalp hair, an advanced expression of the same autoimmune process as patchy alopecia areata. The follicles are usually preserved rather than destroyed, so regrowth remains biologically possible — yet it must be said honestly that response rates in totalis are considerably lower than in patchy disease, and no treatment of any system reliably reverses it. Care here combines constitutional prescribing with support for the significant emotional weight of the condition.

Progression from patchy alopecia areata, sometimes rapid
Eyebrows and lashes may be preserved (their loss suggests universalis)
Nail pitting or ridging in many cases
Scalp skin looks normal — smooth, without scarring

Genetic predisposition, often with a family history of autoimmunity
Association with thyroid disease and vitiligo
Severe stress as a trigger in some cases

Honest discussion of prognosis before treatment begins
Constitutional homeopathic prescribing aimed at the immune picture
Support for the psychological impact, which is never minimised
Practical guidance on scalp protection, and on wigs or coverings for those who want them
Periodic review, with treatment continued only while it is clinically justifiable

Where response occurs it usually begins as fine vellus regrowth in islands. Absence of early response is discussed openly.
Totalis can persist, relapse after regrowth, or occasionally remit even after years. Long-term support is offered without false promises.

faqs.question: What are the realistic chances of regrowth?
faqs.answer: Lower than in patchy alopecia areata, and honesty matters more than optimism here. Spontaneous or treatment-associated regrowth does occur, including after years, but no treatment reliably produces it. We will tell you plainly how your case is responding.

faqs.question: Are my eyebrows at risk too?
faqs.answer: If brows and lashes are also lost the condition is classed as alopecia universalis. Their preservation is a reasonable, though not certain, sign against that progression.

faqs.question: Is wearing a wig giving up?
faqs.answer: Not at all. A well-fitted wig or covering is a legitimate part of living well with totalis, and using one does not interfere with treatment.

name: Alopecia Universalis
summary: The most extensive form of alopecia areata — loss of all scalp and body hair — supported with honest expectations and whole-person care.
intro: Alopecia universalis is the loss of all hair — scalp, brows, lashes and body. It is the most extensive expression of the alopecia areata spectrum and, like totalis, leaves follicles dormant rather than destroyed. Regrowth is biologically possible but response rates are the lowest on the spectrum, and any clinic promising restoration should be treated with caution. Care here is long-term and whole-person: constitutional prescribing, screening for associated autoimmune disease, and unhurried attention to the practical and emotional realities.

Absent nasal hair may increase nose and eye irritation
Nail changes — pitting, ridging, brittleness
Skin otherwise normal, without scarring
Often preceded by patchy or total scalp loss
causes: Autoimmune activity against follicles across the whole body
Strong genetic component
Associated thyroid disease, vitiligo and other autoimmunity
Triggering events are less clear at this severity
treatment: Comprehensive autoimmune screening, coordinated with specialists where indicated
Honest prognosis discussion before any treatment plan
Constitutional homeopathic prescribing

Psychological support, offered as a standing part of care
Reviews that honestly assess whether treatment is helping

expectedResults.detail: Screening and adaptation come first: protecting eyes and skin, and establishing sustainable routines.

faqs.question: Is there any chance of my hair returning?
faqs.answer: Regrowth has been documented even after many years, so the possibility is real — but it is the exception, not the expectation, and no treatment reliably produces it. You deserve that honesty at the outset.

faqs.question: Why do my eyes and nose feel irritated?
faqs.answer: Lashes and nasal hair are filters; without them dust reaches eyes and airways more easily. Wraparound glasses and simple saline care help — practical guidance is part of the consultation.

faqs.question: Is this dangerous to my general health?
faqs.answer: The hair loss itself is not. What matters is screening for associated autoimmune conditions, especially thyroid disease, which is part of care here.

name: Scarring Alopecia (Cicatricial)
summary: A group of conditions in which inflammation destroys the follicle and replaces it with scar tissue — early diagnosis is everything, because scarred areas do not regrow.
intro: Cicatricial (scarring) alopecias share one defining, sobering feature: the inflammation destroys the hair follicle itself, replacing it with scar tissue in which hair cannot regrow. The entire purpose of management is therefore to recognise the process early and halt its spread while follicles remain. Anyone with itching, burning, redness and smooth shiny patches of loss should be assessed promptly — and a scalp biopsy, arranged through dermatology co-care, is often needed for precise diagnosis.
symptoms: Patches of loss where the scalp looks smooth and shiny, without visible follicular openings
Itching, burning or tenderness in and around the patches
Redness or scaling at patch margins while active
Gradual, sometimes stuttering expansion of affected areas
Loss that is permanent within established patches

Discoid lupus erythematosus
Folliculitis decalvans and other neutrophilic conditions
Central centrifugal cicatricial alopecia
Severe untreated infections, burns and radiation
treatment: Prompt assessment of any suspicious patch — speed genuinely matters here
Referral for dermatological co-care and scalp biopsy where diagnosis is uncertain

faqs.question: Will the bald patches fill in again?
faqs.answer: Within truly scarred areas, no — the follicles there are gone, and honesty about this protects you from false promises. At the active margins, where follicles still survive, halting inflammation can preserve them.

faqs.question: Do I really need a biopsy?
faqs.answer: Often, yes. Different scarring alopecias need different management, and they can look alike. A small scalp biopsy, arranged through dermatology, frequently settles the diagnosis.

faqs.question: Can homeopathy alone control this?
faqs.answer: Scarring alopecias often warrant conventional anti-inflammatory treatment, and our care runs alongside it, not instead of it. Sacrificing follicles you can never regrow to test a single approach is not a trade we recommend.

name: Lichen Planopilaris
summary: An inflammatory scarring alopecia with itching, burning and redness around follicles — treated urgently to preserve unaffected hair.
intro: Lichen planopilaris is the follicular form of lichen planus and one of the more common scarring alopecias. Lymphocytic inflammation attacks the upper follicle, producing itch, burning, perifollicular redness and scale, and — if unchecked — permanent patches. Because destroyed follicles cannot be recovered, it is treated as a condition of urgency: dermatological co-care, often with biopsy confirmation, alongside constitutional support.
symptoms: Itching, burning or tenderness of the scalp, often out of proportion to visible change
Redness and fine scale hugging individual follicles
Patchy loss, frequently at the crown and vertex
Smooth, shiny skin within established patches
Sometimes associated lichen planus of skin, nails or mouth
causes: Autoimmune lymphocytic inflammation directed at the follicle
Possible hormonal influence — most patients are middle-aged women
Associations with thyroid autoimmunity
Triggers remain incompletely understood
treatment: Prompt referral for dermatological assessment and biopsy confirmation
Constitutional homeopathic prescribing alongside indicated conventional anti-inflammatories
Scalp comfort measures for itch and burning
Screening for lichen planus elsewhere — mouth, nails, skin
Photographic border-mapping at each review to confirm arrest

expectedResults.detail: Reducing active inflammation is the priority; itch and burning typically ease before anything visible changes.
Stable patch borders on photographs are the marker of success; redness and scale around follicles fade.
Established patches are permanent. The condition can smoulder and reactivate, so periodic surveillance continues after apparent quiet.

faqs.question: Why does my scalp burn when the loss looks small?
faqs.answer: The inflammation sits deep around the follicle, so symptoms often precede and exceed visible loss. Burning and itch are useful early warnings — take them seriously.

faqs.question: Is lichen planopilaris contagious or cancerous?
faqs.answer: Neither. It is an inflammatory autoimmune condition, not an infection or malignancy.

faqs.question: What happens if I wait and watch?
faqs.answer: With scarring alopecias, waiting is the one strategy with an irreversible price: every follicle destroyed during observation is permanent. Early assessment costs little; delay can cost hair you cannot recover.

name: Frontal Fibrosing Alopecia
summary: A progressive band-like recession of the frontal hairline, most often in post-menopausal women, frequently with eyebrow loss — halting progression is the goal.
intro: Frontal fibrosing alopecia is a scarring alopecia, considered a variant of lichen planopilaris, in which the frontal and temporal hairline recedes in a smooth band — often with loss of eyebrows preceding it. It predominantly affects post-menopausal women and has become strikingly more common over recent decades. The receded band is permanent, so the entire aim of care is early recognition and arrest of the advancing edge, usually in co-management with dermatology.
symptoms: Symmetrical band-like recession of the frontal hairline
Pale, smooth skin in the receded band, its follicular openings lost
'Lonely hairs' — isolated survivors ahead of the new hairline
Eyebrow thinning or loss, often the first sign
Itch or redness along the advancing edge in active phases
causes: A lymphocytic scarring process akin to lichen planopilaris
Strong association with the post-menopausal hormonal state
Possible environmental contributors under active research
Occasional family clustering
treatment: Early assessment of any receding band or unexplained eyebrow loss
Dermatological co-care, with biopsy where the picture is unclear
Constitutional homeopathic prescribing alongside indicated conventional care
Gentle skin care for the affected margin; sun protection for exposed skin
Serial photographs of the hairline and brows at every review

expectedResults.detail: Activity at the advancing edge — itch, redness — is settled and baselines photographed.
Success is a hairline that stops receding; measurement, not memory, decides this.

faqs.question: Will my hairline come back?
faqs.answer: The smooth receded band is scarred and will not regrow — the honest goal is stopping further recession. This is exactly why early consultation matters so much.

faqs.question: My eyebrows thinned years before my hairline — related?
faqs.answer: Very possibly. Eyebrow loss precedes hairline recession in a large share of cases and is an important early clue.

faqs.question: Is this caused by sunscreen?
faqs.answer: A debated association exists in research but nothing is proven. We advise balanced sun protection rather than abandoning it, and focus on what demonstrably helps: early arrest of the inflammation.

name: Discoid Lupus Erythematosus (Scalp)
summary: Coin-shaped inflamed, scaly plaques that scar and destroy follicles — an autoimmune condition needing prompt, coordinated care.
intro: Discoid lupus erythematosus is a chronic autoimmune condition of the skin which, on the scalp, produces well-defined inflamed plaques with adherent scale, follicular plugging and pigment change. Left active, the plaques scar and the hair within them is permanently lost. Scalp DLE requires coordinated care — rheumatological or dermatological assessment, photoprotection and monitoring — with constitutional homeopathic support alongside.

Plugged follicles — scale pulling out with a 'carpet-tack' undersurface
Pigment change — darkening at edges, pale centres
Scarred, smooth hair loss within established plaques
Marked sensitivity to sun exposure
causes: Autoimmune inflammation of the skin (a form of cutaneous lupus)
Ultraviolet light as a major trigger and aggravator
Genetic predisposition
Smoking, which worsens the condition and blunts treatment
treatment: Coordinated assessment — dermatology/rheumatology co-care and screening for systemic lupus
Strict, practical photoprotection for the scalp
Constitutional homeopathic prescribing alongside indicated conventional treatment

faqs.question: Is discoid lupus the same as systemic lupus?
faqs.answer: No. DLE is primarily a skin condition; only a minority develop systemic lupus. Periodic screening is done precisely so any change is caught early.

faqs.question: Why is sun protection stressed so much?
faqs.answer: Ultraviolet light is the most reliable trigger of new plaques. A hat and scalp sunscreen are treatment here, not lifestyle advice.

faqs.question: Will the bald patches recover?
faqs.answer: Within scarred plaque centres, no — which is why halting active inflammation early is the entire strategy.

name: Central Centrifugal Cicatricial Alopecia
summary: Scarring hair loss that begins at the crown and spreads outward — most common in women of African descent, and best caught early.
intro: Central centrifugal cicatricial alopecia begins at the crown and expands outward in a slow circle of follicle destruction. It is the most common scarring alopecia in women of African descent, and while its causes are still being clarified, long-term traction and certain chemical or heat practices are suspected contributors in genetically susceptible scalps. As with all scarring alopecias, the central scarred zone is permanent — care aims to halt the advancing margin.
symptoms: Thinning that starts at the crown and spreads outward symmetrically
Scalp in the centre becomes smooth and shiny
Tenderness, tingling or itching, often preceding visible loss
Breakage at the crown as an early warning sign
Slow progression over years
causes: A follicular scarring process with genetic susceptibility
Suspected contribution of long-term traction styling
Possible contribution of chemical relaxers and repeated high heat
Family history in a significant share of cases
treatment: Early assessment of crown thinning, tenderness or persistent breakage
Immediate retirement of traction, relaxer and high-heat practices
Dermatological co-care with biopsy where diagnosis needs confirmation
Constitutional homeopathic prescribing alongside indicated care
Photographic mapping of the margin at every review

expectedResults.detail: Contributing practices stop and active inflammation settles; tenderness and itch ease first.

faqs.question: Did my hairstyle cause this?
faqs.answer: Styling practices are suspected contributors in susceptible scalps rather than the sole cause. Regardless, retiring traction, relaxers and high heat is a necessary part of protecting the hair that remains.

faqs.question: Why is my crown tender before I see loss?
faqs.answer: The inflammation runs deep around follicles, so sensation often precedes visible change. Crown tenderness or tingling with breakage deserves early assessment.

faqs.question: Can the centre regrow if I treat aggressively?
faqs.answer: No treatment recovers scarred follicles, and promises otherwise should raise suspicion. Every effort goes into the margin, where follicles are still alive.

name: Tinea Capitis
summary: Fungal infection of the scalp — scaly patches with broken hairs, most common in children and contagious, requiring properly coordinated treatment.
intro: Tinea capitis is a dermatophyte (ringworm) infection of the scalp, most common in school-age children and readily passed between close contacts. It produces scaly patches with hair broken at or near the surface, sometimes with black dots, and in severe inflammatory cases a boggy swelling called a kerion that risks scarring. One thing is stated without hedging: established tinea capitis requires systemic antifungal treatment under a physician — surface creams cannot reach fungus inside the hair shaft. The clinic coordinates that care and supports recovery.
symptoms: Round scaly patches with hair broken close to the scalp
Black-dot stubble within patches
Itching, sometimes with tender swollen neck glands
In severe cases a boggy, pustular swelling (kerion)
Often other affected children in the household or class
causes: Dermatophyte fungi spread by direct contact
Shared combs, caps, pillows and barber tools
Contact with infected pets in some species
Close-contact settings — schools, hostels, sports
treatment: Prompt diagnosis, with fungal confirmation where available
Coordination of systemic antifungal treatment with your physician — this is non-negotiable for cure
Household measures: no shared combs or headwear, washing of bedding, checking contacts
Supportive homeopathic care for scalp comfort and general resilience
Review to confirm clearance and full regrowth

faqs.question: Can this be cured with creams or oils alone?
faqs.answer: No — the fungus lives inside the hair shaft where surface treatments cannot reach. Established tinea capitis needs a course of oral antifungal medicine under a physician, and we will coordinate exactly that.

faqs.question: Will my child's hair grow back?
faqs.answer: Almost always completely, provided treatment is not delayed. The exception is a severe kerion left untreated, which can scar — one reason speed matters.

faqs.question: How do I stop it spreading at home?
faqs.answer: Separate combs, caps and pillowcases; wash bedding hot; check siblings' scalps; and mention pets, which occasionally carry the fungus.

name: Folliculitis (Scalp)
summary: Itchy or tender pustules around hair follicles — usually bacterial or fungal, uncomfortable, and very treatable once the driver is found.
intro: Scalp folliculitis is inflammation of follicle openings, showing as small pustules or tender red bumps, often along the hairline. Bacteria, yeast overgrowth, occlusion from oils and helmets, and sweat all contribute. It is more uncomfortable than dangerous, but persistent or deep cases deserve proper assessment — recurrent deep folliculitis can damage follicles, and a rarer scarring form (folliculitis decalvans) needs specific care.

Itching, stinging or tenderness
Clusters along the hairline and nape
Crusting where pustules break

Malassezia yeast overgrowth
Occlusion — heavy oils, pomades, helmets, tight caps
Sweat and humid climate
Shaving or friction at the nape

Hygiene and product review — often the decisive step
Homeopathic prescription addressing the recurring tendency
Guidance on helmet and sweat management for Kerala's climate
Escalation to co-managed care if deep or scarring features appear

faqs.question: Is scalp folliculitis contagious?
faqs.answer: Ordinary folliculitis is not meaningfully contagious; it reflects local follicle conditions rather than a spreading infection. Shared towels and razors are still best avoided.

faqs.question: Why does it come back every summer?
faqs.answer: Sweat, humidity and occlusion are its favourite conditions. Adjusting washing frequency and helmet habits for the season usually breaks the cycle.

faqs.question: Should I stop oiling my hair?
faqs.answer: Heavy oil on a folliculitis-prone scalp feeds the problem. Light, wash-out use may be acceptable once settled — guidance is tailored to your scalp at consultation.

name: Folliculitis Decalvans
summary: A rare scarring folliculitis with recurring pustules and 'tufted' hairs — needs early, coordinated care to limit permanent loss.

Because each flare can destroy follicles permanently, it is managed early and in coordination with dermatology.

Strict avoidance of occlusion and scalp trauma

faqs.question: Why do several hairs grow from one spot?

faqs.question: Can homeopathy alone control the flares?
faqs.answer: Active flares generally need conventional antimicrobial treatment, and delaying it costs follicles permanently. Our care runs alongside to address the relapsing tendency, not as a substitute during flares.

faqs.question: Is it curable?
faqs.answer: It is controllable more than curable: with coordinated care, flares become infrequent and scarring stops advancing. Existing scarred patches do not regrow.

name: Seborrheic Dermatitis (Scalp)
summary: Greasy yellow scaling with redness and itch — the inflamed end of the dandruff spectrum, managed for the long game because it relapses.

Genetic tendency

faqs.question: Is this just bad dandruff?

faqs.question: Why does it involve my eyebrows and nose creases?
faqs.answer: Those areas share the same sebum-rich skin the yeast favours. Their involvement actually helps confirm the diagnosis.

faqs.question: Will it cause permanent hair loss?
faqs.answer: By itself, rarely. But sustained inflammation and scratching increase shedding, so controlling it protects density as well as comfort.

faqs.answer: Usually yes — follicles under psoriatic plaques generally survive, and hair regrows as plaques settle. Persistent scratching or forceful scale removal is what risks lasting damage.

faqs.question: Is scalp psoriasis contagious?
faqs.answer: No. It is an immune condition, not an infection — it cannot be passed to anyone.

faqs.question: Why does it flare after a sore throat?
faqs.answer: Streptococcal throat infections are a recognised trigger for some forms of psoriasis. Mentioning recent infections at consultation genuinely changes management.

Follow-ups tracking flare frequency and sleep

expectedResults.detail: Itch intensity drops as trigger products are removed and treatment begins; sleep improves.
Dryness and flaking settle; scratch damage heals.
The atopic tendency is constitutional; management lengthens calm phases, and hair recovery follows scalp calm.

faqs.question: Why does every shampoo irritate me?
faqs.answer: An atopic barrier lets irritants through that intact skin keeps out. The answer is fewer, blander products — not a longer search for the perfect one.

faqs.question: Is my hair fall caused by the eczema?
faqs.answer: Largely indirectly: scratching breaks hair and inflammation increases shedding. As the itch settles, hair generally recovers.

faqs.question: Can children with scalp eczema be treated?
faqs.answer: Yes — childhood atopic scalps respond well to gentle, patient care, and paediatric consultations are routine at this clinic.

name: Contact Dermatitis (Scalp)
summary: Itch, redness or burning after a hair product — irritant or allergic reactions on the scalp, solved by identifying the culprit.
intro: Contact dermatitis of the scalp is a reaction to something applied to it — either direct irritation or true allergy. Hair dye (especially PPD), fragrances and preservatives in shampoos, and some oils are frequent culprits. The pattern is often the giveaway: involvement of the hairline, ears and neck where products run, and timing that follows application. The definitive treatment is not a medicine but detective work — finding and removing the cause.
symptoms: Itch, burning or stinging after product use
Redness, swelling or blistering in allergic reactions — classically after hair dye
Involvement of hairline, ear rims and neck where product runs
Flaking or weeping in established reactions
Clear timing relationship with a product
causes: Hair dye chemicals, especially paraphenylenediamine (PPD)
Fragrances and preservatives in shampoos and conditioners
Some herbal or essential-oil preparations
Cumulative irritation from harsh surfactants
Occupational exposures — salon workers especially
treatment: Structured product history matching timing to exposures
Elimination and reintroduction to confirm the culprit
Referral for patch testing in unclear or recurrent cases
Homeopathic support for skin recovery and reactive tendency
Guidance on safe alternatives, including dye practices

expectedResults.detail: With the culprit removed, acute reactions settle rapidly; severe dye reactions are triaged for urgent care.
Skin barrier recovers; residual flaking and sensitivity resolve.
Avoidance keeps it away; confirmed allergies (like PPD) are permanent, so alternatives are agreed and documented for you.

faqs.question: I've used the same dye for years — can I suddenly react?
faqs.answer: Yes. Allergic sensitisation builds with repeated exposure, so a product tolerated for years can begin reacting. PPD in dark dyes is the classic example.

faqs.question: Is a home 'patch test' before dyeing reliable?
faqs.answer: It catches some but not all reactions, and severe sensitisation can still surprise. After any true dye reaction, formal patch testing and PPD-free alternatives are the safe route.

faqs.question: How fast will it settle once I stop the product?
faqs.answer: Irritant reactions often calm within days; allergic ones take longer. If your scalp is not clearly improving within two weeks of strict avoidance, the culprit hunt continues.

name: Trichorrhexis Nodosa
summary: Weak points along the hair shaft that fracture like brush bristles — the commonest cause of breakage, and usually a damage story with a happy ending.
intro: Trichorrhexis nodosa is the most common hair shaft defect: tiny weak nodes form along the shaft where the cuticle has been damaged, and the hair snaps there, leaving broom-like ends. In most adults it is acquired — the arithmetic of heat, chemicals, tight styling and rough handling — and it responds gratifyingly to changed habits, because the new hair emerging from the follicle is normal. Rare congenital forms exist and are assessed differently.
symptoms: Hair that breaks rather than sheds — short snapped lengths without root bulbs
Tiny whitish nodes visible along shafts
Rough, frayed, broom-like broken ends
Patches of short broken hair where handling is roughest
Hair that 'never grows' — in truth, it breaks as fast as it grows
causes: Chemical processing — relaxers, bleach, repeated colouring
Heat styling
Tight styles and rough brushing, especially of wet hair
Vigorous towel-drying and over-washing
Rarely, congenital shaft fragility or metabolic causes in children
treatment: Confirmation that breakage, not shedding, is the story — the treatments differ completely
A written, realistic hair-handling protocol: what stops, what replaces it
Assessment for any underlying scalp condition driving scratching
Nutritional review where hair quality is globally poor
Progress tracked by breakage length and node visibility, not fall counts

expectedResults.detail: Damaging practices stop; existing damage remains but stops multiplying.
Breakage rate falls sharply; snapped patches begin catching up.
New, structurally normal growth replaces damaged lengths; apparent 'growth' resumes because hair finally outpaces breakage.

faqs.question: Why does my hair never get longer?
faqs.answer: Because it is breaking at the same rate it grows. Stop the breakage and length returns — the follicles were producing normal hair all along.

faqs.question: Is any product able to repair the nodes?
faqs.answer: No product genuinely repairs a fractured shaft; conditioners only reduce further friction. The real fix is new growth under kinder handling.

faqs.question: My child has this all over — same cause?
faqs.answer: Widespread shaft fragility in a young child can occasionally signal a congenital or metabolic cause and deserves proper assessment rather than assumptions about handling.

name: Monilethrix
summary: A genetic beading of the hair shaft that breaks short, usually from infancy — managed with protection and honest, long-term support.
intro: Monilethrix is an inherited hair shaft disorder in which the shaft forms alternating thick and thin segments — beading — and fractures at the constrictions. It typically appears in infancy or early childhood as short, stubbly, fragile hair, often worst at the nape and areas of friction, sometimes with rough follicular bumps. As a genetic keratin condition it cannot be cured; severity varies widely, often improves somewhat after puberty, and management centres on protecting the fragile shaft.
symptoms: Short, brittle hair present from infancy or early childhood
Beaded appearance of shafts under magnification
Breakage concentrated at friction areas — nape, occiput
Rough, keratotic follicular bumps on the scalp
Family history in a parent or sibling is common
causes: Mutations in hair keratin genes, usually dominantly inherited
Severity varies even within one family
Friction and styling stress aggravate breakage on the fragile shaft
treatment: Clinical confirmation, with dermatology co-assessment where diagnosis is unsettled
A friction-minimising care protocol appropriate to the child's age
Constitutional homeopathic support; general health optimised so hair fragility is not compounded
Honest counselling with the family about the genetic nature and variable course
Long-term follow-up through childhood, watching for the common post-pubertal improvement

expectedResults.detail: Protective routine established; breakage at friction sites reduces.
Length achievable within the condition's limits improves with sustained protection; the underlying fragility remains.
Many cases soften considerably after puberty — a genuine, biology-based hope offered honestly, without guarantee.

faqs.question: Is monilethrix curable?
faqs.answer: No — it is a genetic keratin condition. That said, severity varies enormously, protection meaningfully improves what is achievable, and many cases improve after puberty.

faqs.question: Will my other children have it?
faqs.answer: With the usual dominant inheritance, each child of an affected parent has about a fifty per cent chance, though severity is unpredictable. A careful family history is part of the assessment.

faqs.question: Does cutting the hair short help?
faqs.answer: Practically, often yes — shorter hair suffers less friction and looks fuller. It changes nothing biologically but reduces daily breakage.

name: Pili Torti
summary: Flattened, twisted hair shafts that glint unevenly and break easily — congenital or acquired, and occasionally a pointer to associated conditions.
intro: In pili torti the hair shaft is flattened and twisted at intervals along its length, catching light with a distinctive spangled glint and fracturing easily. It may be an isolated congenital finding, part of certain syndromes (some involving hearing), or acquired later alongside scarring scalp conditions or certain medications. Assessment therefore has two jobs: protecting the fragile hair, and checking whether the twisting is a signpost to something broader — including a hearing check in early-onset cases.
symptoms: Fragile hair with patchy short breakage
A spangled, uneven glint along shafts in good light
Flattened, twisted segments under magnification
Onset either in early childhood or newly in adult life
Occasionally associated hearing or other congenital findings
causes: Congenital forms, isolated or syndromic
Association with some inherited conditions, including forms with deafness
Acquired twisting alongside scarring alopecias
Certain medications (notably some retinoids)
Nutritional deficiency states in rare cases
treatment: Confirmation by examination, with co-assessment where syndromic features are possible
Hearing assessment recommended in early-onset cases
Review of medications and nutrition in acquired cases
Friction-minimising hair care protocol
Constitutional homeopathic support and follow-up appropriate to the underlying picture

expectedResults.detail: Protection reduces breakage; any indicated screening (hearing, associated conditions) is completed.
Acquired cases may improve as underlying causes are addressed; congenital fragility persists but managed hair achieves better length.
Care is tailored to the underlying diagnosis; isolated congenital cases often soften with age.

faqs.question: Why would a hair problem need a hearing test?
faqs.answer: Certain congenital forms of pili torti travel with inner-ear conditions (such as Björnstad syndrome). A simple hearing check in early-onset cases is prudent and often reassuring.

faqs.question: Can twisted hair become normal again?
faqs.answer: Acquired pili torti can improve when its cause — medication, deficiency, scalp inflammation — is corrected. Congenital forms persist, though severity often eases with age and protection.

faqs.question: Is the glinting appearance diagnostic?
faqs.answer: It is suggestive — flattened twists reflect light irregularly — but confirmation is by examining shafts under magnification.

name: Bubble Hair
summary: Gas bubbles blown inside the hair shaft by extreme heat on damp hair — sudden patchy breakage with one cause and one fix.
intro: Bubble hair is pure physics: when very hot styling tools meet damp hair, water inside the shaft turns to steam and blows bubbles in the cortex. The shaft becomes brittle and snaps, typically producing a sudden patch of broken, oddly textured hair after one aggressive styling session. Under the microscope the bubbles are unmistakable. It is entirely acquired, entirely preventable, and — because follicles are untouched — fully recoverable.
symptoms: Sudden localised patch of broken, brittle hair
Distinct change of texture — dry, rough, crinkled — in the affected zone
History of high-heat tool use on damp hair, often a single memorable session
Broken shafts without root bulbs
Bubbles within the shaft on microscopy
causes: High-temperature irons or dryers applied to damp hair
Faulty or unregulated heating tools running hotter than indicated
Repeated maximal-heat styling as a routine
treatment: Confirmation of the diagnosis and exclusion of co-existing shaft damage
Retirement of the damaging heat practice — the entire cure
Trim of the irreversibly damaged lengths
Guidance on genuinely safe heat styling: dry hair, regulated temperature
Reassurance: follicles are unaffected and regrowth is normal

expectedResults.detail: The practice stops; damaged lengths are trimmed to prevent ongoing splitting.
Normal new growth emerges — the follicle was never involved.
The patch catches up with surrounding hair; full recovery is the norm.

faqs.question: Will the affected patch recover completely?
faqs.answer: Yes. Bubble hair damages the shaft, not the follicle, so replacement growth is normal. The damaged lengths themselves cannot be repaired — they grow out or are trimmed.

faqs.question: My straightener has a temperature dial — am I safe?
faqs.answer: Only if the hair is properly dry and the tool accurate. 'Damp-plus-maximum-heat' is the classic recipe; a heat-protectant and moderate settings on dry hair avoid it.

faqs.question: How is this different from ordinary heat damage?
faqs.answer: Ordinary heat damage roughens the cuticle gradually; bubble hair is an acute steam injury inside the shaft — faster, more brittle, and usually traceable to specific sessions.

name: Trichoptilosis (Split Ends)
summary: Longitudinal splitting of the hair tip — the universal wear-and-tear sign, and a useful indicator of how hair is being treated.
intro: Trichoptilosis — split ends — is longitudinal fraying of the oldest part of the shaft, where the protective cuticle has finally been worn away by years of washing, friction, heat and chemistry. Universal in long hair to some degree, its extent is a fair audit of hair-care habits. Splits cannot be sealed by any product, only removed and prevented; the real value of a split-end consultation is uncovering the handling pattern producing them prematurely.
symptoms: Frayed, forked or feathered hair tips
Splits travelling upward, sometimes mid-shaft in severe cases
Rough texture and tangling at the ends
White dots at fracture points
Ends looking thin and transparent relative to roots
causes: Cumulative mechanical wear — brushing, friction, tight bands
Heat styling and chemical processing
Sun and hard-water exposure
Washing habits that strip the cuticle
Simple age of the hair fibre — ends are years old
treatment: Handling audit to find why wear is outpacing normal
Sensible trimming schedule to stop splits travelling
Protective-handling protocol: detangling, drying, night care
Assessment for any co-existing shaft disorder when severity is unusual
Nutritional review when overall hair quality is low

expectedResults.detail: Existing splits are trimmed — the only true removal — and the causal habits change.
New end-wear slows dramatically; tangling and roughness reduce.
Ends remain intact between trims; achievable length increases because hair stops eroding from the tip.

faqs.question: Do split-end serums repair the splits?
faqs.answer: No — they temporarily glue and smooth, which reduces snagging, but the fibre remains split. Trimming removes them; changed handling prevents them.

faqs.question: How often should I actually trim?
faqs.answer: Enough to remove damage before it travels: for most, every eight to twelve weeks lightly. With protective handling, the interval stretches naturally.

faqs.question: Why are my ends splitting within months of a cut?
faqs.answer: That speed points to an active cause — heat, harsh surfactants, friction or chemical stress — rather than normal wear. Finding it is the consultation's real job.

name: Trichotillomania
summary: A hair-pulling condition — a recognised body-focused repetitive behaviour, met here without judgement and managed alongside psychological care.
intro: Trichotillomania is recurrent pulling of one's own hair, producing patches of irregular loss with broken hairs of varying length. It is a recognised body-focused repetitive behaviour — a neurobiological condition, not a habit of 'weak will' — often beginning in adolescence and frequently hidden for years behind shame that it does not deserve. Care at this clinic is explicitly non-judgemental: evidence-based psychological therapy (particularly habit reversal training) is the mainstay, with constitutional homeopathic support alongside, and follicles usually recover when pulling stops.
symptoms: Patches of loss with broken hairs of many different lengths
Irregular, angular patch outlines, often within easy reach of the dominant hand
Tension before pulling and relief after, in many though not all
Rituals around the pulled hair
Concealment — styles, scarves, avoidance of salons
Brows and lashes may be involved
causes: A body-focused repetitive behaviour with neurobiological basis
Onset commonly in adolescence
Stress, anxiety and idle/absorbed states as triggers
Frequently co-existing anxiety or mood symptoms
Family history of similar behaviours in some
treatment: An unhurried, explicitly non-judgemental assessment
Referral to and coordination with psychological therapy — habit reversal training has the best evidence
Constitutional homeopathic support for anxiety and tension alongside
Practical strategies: awareness logging, barriers, competing responses
Follow-up that tracks pulling-free progress kindly, expecting and accommodating relapse

expectedResults.detail: Trust first: mapping triggers and situations without shame, and connecting with appropriate therapy.
Pull-free periods lengthen with awareness and competing-response work; regrowth appears in rested patches.
Relapse is part of the condition, not failure. Long-standing intense pulling can occasionally leave permanent thinning, which is why early support matters.

faqs.question: Is hair-pulling just a bad habit I should control?
faqs.answer: No — it is a recognised medical condition with a neurobiological basis. Willpower framing produces only shame; structured therapy genuinely helps.

faqs.question: Will the hair grow back?
faqs.answer: Usually yes once pulling stops, though regrowth takes months and may at first look different. Very long-standing intense pulling can permanently damage some follicles — one reason early help matters.

faqs.question: I do it without noticing — does that still count?
faqs.answer: Yes. 'Automatic' pulling during absorbed states is one of the two classic patterns, and awareness training is designed exactly for it.

name: Trichophagia
summary: Swallowing pulled hair — a companion to hair-pulling that carries a real medical risk (hairball obstruction) and deserves prompt, kind attention.
intro: Trichophagia is the swallowing of pulled hair, occurring in a subset of people with trichotillomania. It matters medically far beyond the scalp: swallowed hair cannot be digested and can accumulate over years into a trichobezoar — a gastric hairball — capable of causing pain, vomiting and dangerous obstruction (including the 'Rapunzel syndrome' extension into the intestine). Care is therefore twofold: the same non-judgemental behavioural support as trichotillomania, plus explicit safety-netting so any warning symptom is investigated without delay.
symptoms: Hair-pulling accompanied by mouthing or swallowing the hair
Often concealed even more deeply than pulling itself
Warning signs of accumulation: upper abdominal pain or fullness, nausea, vomiting, early satiety, weight loss
Sometimes a palpable upper-abdominal mass in advanced cases
Most common in adolescent girls, though not exclusive
causes: A body-focused repetitive behaviour on the trichotillomania spectrum
Oral-ritual component of the pulling cycle
Frequently co-existing anxiety; occasionally iron deficiency and pica-like features
Concealment delaying detection
treatment: Direct but kind screening — everyone with hair-pulling is asked about swallowing, because hiding it is the norm
Immediate referral for abdominal assessment if any warning symptom exists — bezoars are a surgical problem, not a homeopathic one
Coordination with psychological therapy for the underlying behaviour
Iron and nutritional screening
Family education on warning signs, with a clear plan for urgent care

expectedResults.detail: Safety first: symptom screening and, where indicated, urgent referral for imaging. This precedes everything else.
Behavioural therapy addresses the pulling-swallowing cycle; swallowing typically stops alongside pulling.
Continued vigilance for abdominal symptoms with an agreed action plan; behavioural relapse is met with support, not blame.

faqs.question: Is swallowed hair really dangerous?
faqs.answer: It can be. Hair is indigestible and accumulates; a large bezoar can obstruct the stomach or intestine and require surgery. Persistent abdominal pain, vomiting or early fullness in anyone who swallows hair needs prompt hospital assessment — please do not wait for a clinic appointment.

faqs.question: My daughter chews her hair but I'm not sure she swallows — should I worry?
faqs.answer: Chewing often precedes swallowing and both belong on the same spectrum. Raise it gently and have it assessed; early, kind intervention is far easier than late.

faqs.question: Can homeopathy dissolve a hairball?
faqs.answer: No, and no honest practitioner will claim otherwise. Established bezoars need endoscopic or surgical management; our role is the behavioural side and coordination of proper care.

name: Traction Alopecia
summary: Hair loss from sustained pulling by tight styles — fully reversible early, permanent late, so timing is everything.
intro: Traction alopecia is mechanical: styles that pull — tight ponytails and buns, braids, extensions, tightly wrapped styles — exert chronic tension that first inflames and eventually destroys follicles along the lines of pull, classically the frontal and temporal margins. Its course has a clean fork: caught early, it is among the most fully reversible hair losses; sustained for years, the follicles scar and the loss becomes permanent. The treatment is not subtle, but it is non-negotiable — the tension must stop.
symptoms: Thinning along the hairline and temples following the style's pull lines
'Fringe sign' — a preserved line of fine hairs at the very edge
Tender scalp, bumps or pustules after tight styling
Broken short hairs where tension is greatest
In long-standing cases, smooth shiny skin — the scarring stage
causes: Tight ponytails, buns, braids and cornrows
Extensions and weaves adding constant weight
Tightly wrapped or pinned religious and occupational head coverings
Rollers worn overnight
Repeated pulling styles begun in childhood
treatment: Honest identification of the responsible styles — and workable, culturally respectful alternatives
Complete rest from tension for the recovery period
Assessment of stage: soreness and bumps suggest recoverable; smooth skin warns of scarring
Constitutional homeopathic support for follicle recovery
Photographic review of the margins at each visit

expectedResults.detail: Tension stops; tenderness and folliculitis settle.
Early-stage cases show regrowth at the margins — first fine, then thickening.
Recovery continues where follicles survived; areas already scarred (smooth, shiny) do not return, said plainly at the outset.

faqs.question: How tight is too tight?
faqs.answer: If a style hurts, lifts the skin, or leaves your scalp tender that evening, it is causing traction. Pain is the follicle's complaint, not a styling norm to endure.

faqs.question: I can't abandon braiding for cultural reasons — what then?
faqs.answer: Looser tension, larger sections, shorter wear periods, rest weeks between installs and avoiding extensions on the fragile hairline achieve most of the protection while respecting the style tradition.

faqs.question: Will my temples fill back in?
faqs.answer: If the skin there still shows follicular openings and stubble, prospects are good over six to twelve months of rest. Smooth shiny skin means scarring, and those areas will not regrow — the reason to act now.

name: Friction Alopecia
summary: Hair thinning where something rubs — helmets, pillows, straps, socks — resolving when the rubbing stops.
intro: Friction alopecia is loss from chronic rubbing rather than pulling: the zone under a daily helmet strap, the back of the head in infants and bed-bound patients, the ankle line above tight socks, areas rubbed by rough pillowcases. Repeated friction wears and breaks the shaft and, over long periods, can miniaturise follicles. It is usually reversible once the rubbing stops, and the diagnosis is often made simply by matching the thinned zone to the object that touches it daily.
symptoms: Thinning or breakage precisely where an object rubs
Helmet-band pattern around the head in daily riders
Occipital patch in infants and the bed-bound
Sock-line loss on the lower legs
Rough, broken shafts within the zone rather than shed bulbs
causes: Daily helmet or cap wear with movement against hair
Sleeping friction — coarse fabrics, restless surfaces
Tight sock or clothing lines
Habitual rubbing or leaning
Occupational headgear
treatment: Matching the loss map to daily friction sources — usually decisive
Interruption of the friction: liners, fit adjustment, smoother fabrics
Hair-care support while the zone recovers
Assessment for co-existing causes if the map does not fully fit
Review to confirm regrowth once friction is controlled

expectedResults.detail: Friction source is modified; breakage in the zone slows.
Regrowth fills the zone in most cases; infant occipital patches resolve as sleeping patterns mature.
Long-standing intense friction occasionally leaves partial thinning; prevention is built into the daily routine.

faqs.question: I must wear a helmet daily — am I stuck with this?
faqs.answer: No. A smooth balaclava-style liner, correct fit so the helmet moves with the head, and drying sweat promptly remove most of the friction while keeping you safe. Do not stop wearing the helmet.

faqs.question: Is my baby's bald patch at the back a problem?
faqs.answer: Almost never — occipital friction loss in infants is normal and resolves as they sit up and sleep patterns mature. Persistent or expanding patches beyond that age can be reviewed.

faqs.question: How is this different from traction loss?
faqs.answer: Traction pulls at the root along style lines; friction rubs the shaft where surfaces touch. The maps differ, and so does the fix — release tension versus remove rubbing.

name: PCOS-related Hair Loss
summary: Scalp thinning driven by the androgen excess of polycystic ovary syndrome — often while unwanted facial hair increases — treated through the hormonal picture.
intro: In polycystic ovary syndrome, elevated androgens act on hair in two opposite ways at once: scalp follicles at the parting and crown miniaturise, while facial and body hair coarsens. Insulin resistance frequently amplifies the process. Treating the scalp alone misses the point; care addresses the hormonal and metabolic picture — cycles, androgens, insulin — alongside the hair, coordinated with gynaecology where needed.
symptoms: Thinning at the crown and parting with a preserved hairline
Coincident increase in facial or body hair
Irregular, delayed or absent periods
Acne along jawline and chin
Weight gain that resists effort
Skin tags or darkened skin folds suggesting insulin resistance
causes: Elevated androgen levels acting on sensitive scalp follicles
Insulin resistance amplifying androgen effects
Genetic predisposition to both PCOS and pattern sensitivity
Weight and lifestyle factors in a two-way loop
Chronic stress affecting hormonal rhythm
treatment: Full menstrual, weight and hormonal history with review of ultrasound and lab reports
Testing where gaps exist — androgens, insulin markers, thyroid, ferritin (deficiencies co-travel)
Constitutional homeopathic prescribing for the hormonal picture
Practical insulin-resistance work: food pattern, movement, sleep
Coordination with your gynaecologist, especially if conception is planned
Photographic tracking of parting width alongside cycle regularity

expectedResults.detail: The hormonal picture is clarified and treatment begun; cycles and skin usually respond before hair.
Shedding settles as the internal environment steadies; cycle regularity is the objective marker.
Parting density improves where follicles remained viable — reviewed photographically. PCOS is managed long-term, not cured.

faqs.question: Why is hair falling from my head but growing on my face?
faqs.answer: Both are androgen effects: scalp follicles miniaturise under androgens while facial follicles are stimulated by them. Improving the hormonal picture addresses both directions.

faqs.question: Will losing weight really help my hair?
faqs.answer: In PCOS with insulin resistance, even modest weight change measurably lowers androgen drive and often improves cycles first, hair after. It is one of the few levers entirely in your hands.

faqs.question: I want to conceive — does that change treatment?
faqs.answer: Yes, tell us at the first visit. Plans are made pregnancy-compatible and coordinated with your gynaecologist from the start.

name: Menopausal Hair Loss
summary: Thinning through perimenopause and beyond, as falling oestrogen unmasks androgen effects — supported through the transition with realistic goals.
intro: Around menopause the hormonal shelter that oestrogen gave hair is withdrawn: relative androgen influence rises, growth phases shorten, and many women notice widening partings, slower growth and texture change, sometimes with new facial hair. It arrives amid sleep disruption, stress and frequently overlooked thyroid or iron issues of the same life stage — so assessment untangles all contributors rather than blaming 'age' and stopping there.
symptoms: Gradual thinning at crown and parting through perimenopause
Slower growth and finer, drier texture
Increased shedding episodes during the transition years
Sometimes new chin or facial hair
Often accompanied by disturbed sleep, flushes and fatigue
causes: Declining oestrogen unmasking androgen effects on sensitive follicles
Age-related follicular slowing
Thyroid dysfunction — common at the same age and frequently missed
Iron and vitamin D insufficiency
Sleep disruption and stress of the transition
treatment: Assessment separating hormonal-transition effects from co-existing treatable causes
Testing: thyroid profile, ferritin, vitamin D as a minimum
Constitutional homeopathic prescribing for the transition as a whole — sleep, flushes and hair together
Nutritional support appropriate to the life stage, including protein adequacy
Photographic tracking with honest, realistic goals

expectedResults.detail: Co-existing correctables are found and fixed; sleep and general wellbeing usually improve first.
Shedding settles; texture and breakage improve.
The goal is preserving and modestly improving density through the transition — full restoration of decades-past volume is not promised, because it would be a false promise.

faqs.question: Is thinning inevitable after menopause?
faqs.answer: Some change is common, but the degree varies enormously and is frequently worsened by treatable co-factors — low ferritin, thyroid drift, poor sleep. Addressing those changes the trajectory.

faqs.question: Why treat sleep and flushes at a hair consultation?
faqs.answer: Because the same transition drives them all, and constitutional treatment addresses the person, not one symptom. Hair rarely improves while sleep is wrecked.

faqs.question: Will my hair return to what it was at thirty?
faqs.answer: Honestly, no — and any clinic promising that deserves scepticism. Meaningful goals are stopping excess loss, improving quality and density, and protecting what you have long-term.

name: Thyroid-related Alopecia
summary: Diffuse hair loss from an underactive or overactive thyroid — one blood test away from an answer, with recovery that lags months behind treatment.
intro: Both hypo- and hyperthyroidism disturb the hair cycle, producing diffuse loss across the scalp — classically with dry coarse hair and outer-eyebrow thinning when underactive, fine limp hair when overactive. Because follicles are among the fastest-dividing tissues, hair often signals thyroid trouble before the classic symptoms are recognised. The cardinal rules here: test properly, never adjust thyroid medication except through the prescribing physician, and understand that hair recovery lags months behind normalised blood results.
symptoms: Diffuse thinning across the whole scalp, not patches
Loss of the outer third of the eyebrows (hypothyroid pattern)
Dry, coarse, brittle hair — or fine and limp in overactivity
Accompanying fatigue, temperature intolerance, weight or cycle changes
Slow regrowth even after levels normalise — the expected lag
causes: Hypothyroidism, including autoimmune Hashimoto's thyroiditis
Hyperthyroidism, including Graves' disease
Post-partum thyroiditis, often missed
Associated alopecia areata risk with autoimmune thyroid disease
Occasionally, initial months of thyroid treatment itself
treatment: Proper testing — TSH with free T3/T4, and anti-TPO antibodies where autoimmunity is suspected
Review of existing reports; borderline results reinterpreted in the hair context
Absolute rule: thyroid medication is adjusted only by the prescribing physician
Constitutional homeopathic care for associated symptoms and the autoimmune tendency
Ferritin and vitamin D screening — deficiencies commonly co-exist and stall recovery
Patience built into follow-up: hair lags labs by three to six months

expectedResults.detail: Diagnosis completed and thyroid management optimised with your physician; energy and general symptoms respond first.
Shedding settles once levels stabilise.
Regrowth and density visibly recover — reliably behind the blood results, which is expected and not failure.

faqs.question: My thyroid reports normalised but hair is still falling — why?
faqs.answer: Because hair works on a months-long cycle: it lags behind blood results by three to six months. Continued shedding shortly after normalisation is expected; persistent loss beyond that window is re-investigated for co-factors like low ferritin.

faqs.question: Can I stop thyroxine now that I'm taking homeopathic treatment?
faqs.answer: No. Thyroid hormone replacement is adjusted only by the physician who prescribed it, based on blood tests. Stopping it abruptly is genuinely dangerous, and no one at this clinic will ever advise it.

faqs.question: Which tests should I bring?
faqs.answer: TSH, free T3 and free T4 as a base; anti-TPO antibodies if autoimmune disease is suspected; plus ferritin and vitamin D, which so often travel alongside. And pause high-dose biotin three days before testing — it distorts thyroid assays.

name: Iron Deficiency Hair Loss
summary: Diffuse shedding from depleted iron stores — where ferritin, not haemoglobin, tells the truth, and correction must be test-guided.
intro: Iron deficiency is among the most common — and most commonly missed — drivers of diffuse hair loss, because a normal haemoglobin does not exclude it. The body defends red blood cells first: tissue iron stores (measured as ferritin) empty long before anaemia appears, and follicles, as fast-dividing 'non-essential' tissue, feel it early. Menstruating women, vegetarians and frequent blood donors are most at risk. The rules are simple: test ferritin specifically, correct guided by results, and never supplement blind — iron overload is genuinely harmful.
symptoms: Diffuse shedding across the scalp
Fatigue, poor exercise tolerance, breathlessness on stairs
Brittle nails, sometimes spoon-shaped
Pale inner eyelids, cravings for ice or unusual substances
Restless legs at night in some
'Normal blood test' history where ferritin was never actually measured
causes: Menstrual blood loss, especially heavy cycles
Low dietary iron — vegetarian diets need deliberate planning
Poor absorption: tea/coffee with meals, antacids, gut conditions
Pregnancy and breastfeeding demands
Frequent blood donation
Unrecognised gastrointestinal loss — investigated when unexplained
treatment: Specific testing: serum ferritin, not just haemoglobin — with inflammation markers where needed, since ferritin rises falsely during inflammation
Investigation of the cause of deficiency, not just the number — heavy cycles and gut losses deserve attention
Test-guided iron correction with absorption coaching: vitamin C alongside, tea/coffee/calcium away from doses
Dietary pattern rebuilt for sustained iron adequacy
Constitutional homeopathic support
Ferritin re-checked at intervals; hair reviewed photographically with the expected lag explained

expectedResults.detail: Deficiency confirmed and correction begun; energy typically improves well before hair.
Shedding settles as stores rebuild.
Density visibly recovers, lagging the ferritin by months — expected biology, not treatment failure.

faqs.question: My haemoglobin is normal — how can I be iron deficient?
faqs.answer: Because haemoglobin is defended to the last: stores (ferritin) empty first, and hair suffers during that hidden stage. Ferritin is the number that matters for hair.

faqs.question: What ferritin level should I aim for?
faqs.answer: Laboratory 'normal' often starts near 12–15 ng/mL — a threshold for anaemia, not an optimum for hair. Correction targets are set individually and rechecked, rather than chasing a single magic number.

faqs.question: Can I just start iron tablets myself?
faqs.answer: Please don't. Iron overload harms the liver and heart, some people carry haemochromatosis unknowingly, and blind supplementation can also mask a bleeding source that needed investigating. Test first, correct under guidance.

name: Zinc Deficiency Hair Loss
summary: Shedding with slow healing, taste changes and skin trouble — zinc deficiency affects hair among much else, and responds to careful correction.
intro: Zinc sits in hundreds of enzymes, including those building keratin, so deficiency shows in hair (diffuse shedding, brittle texture), skin (rashes around mouth and eyes, slow wound healing), nails (white spots, ridges) and even taste. It arises from restrictive or phytate-heavy diets, absorption problems, pregnancy, and prolonged illness. Correction works — but more is not better: excess zinc induces copper deficiency, so supplementation is dosed and time-limited, never open-ended.
symptoms: Diffuse hair shedding with brittle, lustreless texture
White spots or ridging on nails
Rashes around mouth, eyes or in skin folds
Slow wound healing, frequent minor infections
Blunted taste or smell
In children: appetite loss and faltering growth
causes: Low intake — restrictive diets, low animal-protein patterns
High-phytate staples binding zinc in the gut
Malabsorption: gut disease, long-term acid suppression
Pregnancy and breastfeeding demands
Alcohol excess, chronic illness
Rarely, genetic zinc transport defects in infants
treatment: Clinical assessment with serum zinc where indicated — interpreted cautiously, as blood levels are imperfect
Dietary rebuild: realistic zinc-adequate eating for your food pattern
Dosed, time-limited supplementation where warranted — never indefinite, to protect copper status
Correction of absorption obstacles
Constitutional homeopathic support
Review of skin, nails and shedding as the visible markers of progress

expectedResults.detail: Skin symptoms and taste usually respond first; healing quickens.
Shedding settles; nail growth emerges without new white marks.
Hair density and texture recover with the usual biological lag.

faqs.question: Can a blood test confirm zinc deficiency?
faqs.answer: Serum zinc helps but is imperfect — levels swing with meals, stress and inflammation. Diagnosis leans on the whole picture: diet, symptoms and response to careful correction.

faqs.question: Why not just take a strong zinc supplement long-term?
faqs.answer: Because sustained high-dose zinc causes copper deficiency — itself a cause of anaemia and neurological problems. Zinc correction is dosed and time-limited by design.

faqs.question: Which foods actually help?
faqs.answer: For non-vegetarians: shellfish, meat and eggs. Vegetarian patterns lean on legumes, nuts, seeds and dairy, with soaking/sprouting of grains and pulses to unlock the zinc that phytates bind.

name: Vitamin D Deficiency Hair Loss
summary: Low vitamin D — near-ubiquitous with indoor living — contributes to shedding and stubborn recovery, and is easy to test and correct.
intro: Vitamin D receptors sit in the hair follicle itself, where the vitamin participates in starting new growth cycles; severe receptor defects cause profound hair loss, and low levels are consistently associated with telogen effluvium and alopecia areata. Despite Kerala's sunshine, indoor routines and covered exposure make deficiency remarkably common. It is rarely the sole cause of hair loss — but it is a frequent accomplice that stalls recovery from other causes, and it is cheap to test and straightforward to correct under guidance.
symptoms: Diffuse shedding or slow recovery from another hair condition
Fatigue and low mood
Bone aches, muscle weakness or cramps
Frequent minor infections
Predominantly indoor lifestyle or fully covered sun exposure
causes: Indoor work and life despite a sunny climate
Fully covering clothing limiting skin synthesis
Darker skin requiring longer exposure for the same synthesis
Low dietary sources — few foods carry meaningful vitamin D
Obesity sequestering vitamin D; gut conditions impairing absorption
treatment: Testing 25-hydroxy-vitamin D rather than guessing
Dose-appropriate correction under guidance — massive self-dosing causes real toxicity
A sustainable sun-exposure plan fitted to your routine and skin
Dietary and co-factor review (vitamin D works alongside adequate calcium and magnesium)
Constitutional homeopathic care for the whole picture
Re-testing to confirm repletion, then a maintenance plan

expectedResults.detail: Levels corrected; energy, mood and muscle aches usually respond first.
Shedding settles — particularly where vitamin D was stalling recovery from effluvium or areata.
Hair density recovers with the standard lag; maintenance keeps levels from sliding back.

faqs.question: I live in Kerala — how can I lack vitamin D?
faqs.answer: Sunshine outside the window does not reach skin that is indoors, in vehicles, or fully covered during peak hours. Deficiency is common across sunny India for exactly this reason; testing settles it in a day.

faqs.question: Can vitamin D alone regrow my hair?
faqs.answer: If deficiency was the main brake, correction visibly helps; more often it is one of several factors, and fixing it lets the rest of treatment work. It is rarely the whole story — beware anyone selling it as one.

faqs.question: Is more vitamin D always better?
faqs.answer: No. Vitamin D is fat-soluble and accumulates; aggressive self-dosing causes toxicity with high calcium, kidney strain and — ironically — sometimes hair shedding. Correct to tested levels, under guidance.

name: Protein Deficiency Hair Loss
