summary: Hair is protein — when intake falls short, through dieting or inadequate meals, the body rations follicles first and shedding follows.
intro: Hair shafts are almost entirely keratin, and the body treats hair as expendable: when protein intake falls short — crash diets, poorly planned vegetarian or elderly eating, illness, post-surgical phases — follicles are switched to rest within months and shafts grow finer and weaker. Alongside shedding, texture dulls, nails soften and muscles waste quietly. Recovery is gratifyingly reliable once intake is rebuilt, with the usual months-long lag between the plate and the parting.
symptoms: Increased diffuse shedding two to four months after intake dropped
Hair that grows finer, drier and weaker
Loss of shine; increased breakage
Soft, peeling nails
Reduced muscle strength; puffiness in severe cases
History of crash dieting, tiny meals, or protein-light eating
causes: Crash and fad diets, skipped meals
Vegetarian or vegan patterns without deliberate protein planning
Reduced appetite and intake in the elderly
Post-surgical, bariatric or convalescent phases
Digestive conditions limiting absorption
Athletic training outstripping intake
treatment: Honest dietary assessment — quantities and quality, not just food names
A realistic protein target rebuilt into your actual food culture and budget
Attention to co-travelling deficits: iron, zinc, B12 commonly accompany
Medical review where poor appetite or absorption is the driver
Constitutional homeopathic support for appetite and recovery
Progress tracked by texture, breakage and shedding — then density photographs

expectedResults.detail: Intake rebuilt; energy and satiety improve first.
Shedding settles; new growth at the roots is stronger — often felt before seen.
Density and texture visibly recover as stronger shafts replace weak lengths.

faqs.question: How much protein do I actually need?
faqs.answer: As a working guide, near 0.8–1 g per kilogram of body weight daily for most adults — more in recovery, training or later life. We translate that into your real meals rather than leaving it as a number.

faqs.question: I'm vegetarian — can I fix this without eggs or meat?
faqs.answer: Absolutely, with planning: dal and legumes at every meal, dairy or soy, nuts and seeds, and attention to quantity. Vegetarian is not the problem; unplanned vegetarian is.

faqs.question: I stopped my crash diet — why is hair still falling?
faqs.answer: Because today's shedding reflects the deficit of two to four months ago. With intake restored, expect settling over the coming two to three months, then regrowth behind it.

name: Scalp Acne
summary: Pimples, papules and tender spots along the hairline and crown, where sebum, sweat and hair products meet an occluded follicle.
intro: Scalp acne behaves like acne anywhere else — a follicle blocks, sebum builds up behind it and the surrounding skin inflames — but hair, helmets, oils and infrequent washing make the scalp a particularly easy place for it to persist. Most cases are mild and cosmetic. The ones worth treating properly are those that recur month after month, hurt, or leave the follicle scarred, because repeated deep inflammation is one of the ways hair is permanently lost.
symptoms: Small tender pimples along the hairline, nape and crown
Spots that hurt when the hair is tied, combed or brushed
Occasional larger nodules that take weeks to settle
Greasiness at the roots within a day of washing
Brown or dark marks left behind after a spot heals
Itch or a crawling sensation before a new crop appears
causes: Excess sebum with follicular blockage
Heavy hair oils, serums, gels and leave-in products left on the scalp
Sweat trapped under helmets, caps or long hair tied while damp
Infrequent washing, or washing so often that the scalp overcompensates
Hormonal drivers such as PCOS or an androgen-dominant phase
Bacterial and yeast overgrowth in an already blocked follicle
treatment: Examination of the scalp to separate acne from folliculitis, which is treated differently
Constitutional homeopathic prescription based on the pattern of eruption, discharge and general health
A practical review of oils, styling products and washing frequency
Attention to hormonal or digestive factors when the pattern points that way
Referral for antibiotic or dermatological care where lesions are deep, scarring or spreading

expectedResults.detail: Tenderness and the size of new spots are usually the first things to change.
Crops tend to become smaller and less frequent as sebum production settles.
Marks left by old spots fade slowly over months. Deep, scarred follicles do not regrow hair, which is why early treatment matters.

faqs.question: Should I stop oiling my hair completely?
faqs.answer: Not necessarily. What matters is what is used, how much, and how long it stays on the scalp. Heavy oils left overnight on an acne-prone scalp reliably make it worse; a light application washed out the same day usually does not.

faqs.question: Is scalp acne the same as dandruff?
faqs.answer: No. Dandruff is a scaling condition of the scalp surface; scalp acne is inflammation inside the follicle. They often occur together, which is why the scalp is examined rather than treated by description alone.

name: Acne Keloidalis Nuchae
summary: Firm, keloid-like bumps at the nape of the neck that follow repeated follicular inflammation and can leave permanent bald patches.
intro: Acne keloidalis nuchae begins as small papules or pustules at the back of the neck and along the posterior hairline. Left to recur, the healing skin lays down thickened scar tissue and the follicles inside it are lost for good. It is far more common in men, and strongly associated with close clipping of the hairline. This is one of the conditions where early treatment genuinely changes the outcome, because once a keloidal plaque has formed the hair inside it will not return.
symptoms: Firm, smooth, dome-shaped bumps at the nape of the neck
Itching or a burning sensation over the affected band
Pustules and crusting during active flares
Bumps merging into a raised, hairless plaque over time
Occasional discharge or bleeding when a lesion is picked or shaved over
Tenderness when a collar or helmet strap rubs the area
causes: Repeated close shaving or clipping of the posterior hairline
Friction from collars, helmets and headrests
An individual tendency to keloid formation
Chronic folliculitis in the affected band
Curly hair re-entering the skin after cutting
Delayed treatment of the earliest papular stage
treatment: Careful examination to grade how much of the area is already scarred
Homeopathic prescription directed at the inflammatory and keloidal tendency together
Firm advice on stopping close clipping and razor use over the affected band
Management of friction from helmets, collars and headwear
Early dermatological or surgical referral for established keloidal plaques, where intralesional or surgical treatment is the appropriate option

expectedResults.detail: Itching, burning and the appearance of new pustules are usually the first things to ease.
Active inflammation can quieten considerably, which limits further scarring.
Existing keloidal tissue does not reverse with homeopathic treatment, and hair lost inside it does not return. The realistic goal is to stop the process spreading.

faqs.question: Will the bumps I already have disappear?
faqs.answer: Established keloidal bumps are scar tissue and will not resolve with medicine alone. Treatment aims to stop new ones forming. For existing plaques, intralesional injections or surgical removal by a dermatologist are the options worth discussing.

faqs.question: Can I ever get a haircut again?
faqs.answer: Yes, but not a close clip or razor finish at the nape. Leaving a few millimetres of length and asking the barber not to shave the hairline is the single most useful change most patients make.

name: Dissecting Cellulitis of the Scalp
summary: Deep, boggy, interconnecting nodules on the scalp that discharge and, untreated, destroy the follicles beneath them.
intro: Dissecting cellulitis — also called perifolliculitis capitis abscedens et suffodiens — is an uncommon but serious inflammatory scalp disease. Soft fluctuant swellings form in the deeper scalp, connect underneath the surface via sinus tracts, and discharge pus. It causes real destruction of hair follicles and is classed among the scarring alopecias. It needs prompt, active medical management; homeopathic treatment here is supportive and is not a substitute for that.
symptoms: Boggy, soft swellings on the crown or back of the scalp
Pus or blood-stained discharge from more than one opening
Pressure on one swelling producing discharge from another
Patchy hair loss over and around the affected areas
Pain, tenderness and a foul odour during flares
Smooth, shiny bald areas where old lesions have healed
causes: Follicular occlusion followed by rupture into the deeper scalp
Secondary bacterial infection of the occluded follicles
Association with severe acne and hidradenitis suppurativa in the same person
Immune and inflammatory predisposition
Smoking, which is consistently linked to the follicular occlusion group
Delay in starting effective treatment
treatment: Immediate assessment of extent, discharge and existing scarring
Coordination with a dermatologist — this condition often needs systemic medication
Homeopathic prescription alongside that care for the inflammatory tendency, discharge and general vitality
Attention to associated acne, hidradenitis and smoking
Regular photographic documentation, because progression is what treatment decisions turn on

expectedResults.detail: The first priority is controlling active discharge and pain, usually alongside conventional treatment.
With sustained treatment, flares tend to become less frequent and less extensive.
Areas already scarred stay bald permanently. This is a long-term condition, and relapse after stopping treatment is common.

faqs.question: Can this be treated with homeopathy alone?
faqs.answer: It should not be. Dissecting cellulitis destroys follicles while it is active, and delay costs hair permanently. This clinic treats it alongside dermatological care, not instead of it.

faqs.question: Why does my hair not grow back in the healed patches?
faqs.answer: The inflammation reaches deep enough to destroy the follicle and replace it with scar tissue. Once that has happened there is no follicle left to grow a hair, which is why the aim is to stop new areas being affected.

name: Pityriasis Amiantacea
summary: Thick, asbestos-like scale that binds itself around the hair shafts in sheets, lifting hair with it when it separates.
intro: Pityriasis amiantacea is not a disease in its own right so much as a striking pattern of scaling that sits on top of another scalp condition — most often psoriasis, seborrhoeic dermatitis or eczema. The scale is thick, silvery and clings around the hair shafts rather than flaking free, and hair frequently comes away with it. Identifying and treating the underlying condition is what actually resolves it.
symptoms: Thick, layered, silvery-white scale bound around the hair shafts
Scale that lifts in sheets rather than falling as loose flakes
Hairs coming away attached to the removed scale
Localised patches, often on the crown, rather than whole-scalp flaking
Itching and a tight, uncomfortable scalp
Temporary thinning over the affected patches
causes: Underlying scalp psoriasis
Severe seborrhoeic dermatitis
Atopic or contact eczema of the scalp
Secondary bacterial or fungal colonisation
Tinea capitis in children, which must be excluded before anything else
Aggressive scratching or picking that thickens the plaque further
treatment: Examination to identify the underlying scalp disease — the treatment follows from that
Exclusion of fungal infection, particularly in children
Homeopathic prescription for the underlying condition and the individual's overall pattern
Practical guidance on softening and lifting scale without pulling hair out
Review of any medicated shampoos or topicals already in use

expectedResults.detail: Scale usually becomes softer and easier to lift once the underlying inflammation is being treated.
Patches typically reduce in thickness and extent; itch settles.
Hair lost with the scale generally regrows, since the follicle is not usually destroyed. Recurrence depends on how well the underlying condition is controlled.

faqs.question: Is the hair I lose with the scale gone for good?
faqs.answer: Usually not. In pityriasis amiantacea the follicle itself is generally intact, so hair regrows once the scaling settles. Persistent bald patches suggest a different, scarring process and should be re-examined.

faqs.question: Should I peel the scale off?
faqs.answer: Not dry, and not forcefully — that is how hair gets pulled out and how the skin beneath gets damaged. Softening it first and lifting gently is the approach advised at the consultation.

name: Kerion
summary: A boggy, painful inflamed swelling of the scalp caused by an intense immune reaction to a fungal infection — a medical urgency in children.
intro: A kerion is what happens when the body reacts violently to tinea capitis. The scalp develops a raised, soft, painful swelling studded with pustules, hair falls out easily from it, and lymph nodes in the neck swell. It looks like a bacterial abscess and is frequently mistaken for one. It is a fungal problem, it needs oral antifungal treatment promptly, and delay leads to permanent scarring alopecia. If a child has this, they should be seen quickly.
symptoms: A raised, boggy, tender swelling on the scalp
Pustules and thick crusting over the surface
Hair pulling out painlessly from the affected patch
Swollen, tender lymph nodes in the neck or behind the ears
Fever or general unwellness in some children
A well-defined bald area developing over days rather than months
causes: Dermatophyte fungal infection of the scalp — the underlying tinea capitis
A strong host immune response to that fungus
Delayed or incorrect treatment of scalp ringworm
Contact with an infected child, pet or shared comb, cap or pillow
Topical steroids applied in the mistaken belief it is eczema, which worsens it
treatment: Urgent confirmation of fungal infection and referral for oral antifungal treatment, which is the definitive therapy
Homeopathic support alongside that for pain, inflammation and general recovery
Screening of household contacts and advice on shared combs, caps and pillows
Clear instruction that topical steroid creams are not the answer here
Follow-up to assess how much hair recovers once the infection clears

expectedResults.detail: With antifungal treatment underway, pain, swelling and discharge settle relatively quickly.
The scalp surface heals and hair begins to return over follicles that survived.
Where inflammation was severe or treatment delayed, some scarring and permanent hair loss can remain. Early treatment is the difference.

faqs.question: Can this be treated without antifungal tablets?
faqs.answer: No. Oral antifungals are the established treatment for tinea capitis and kerion, and topical treatment alone does not reach the fungus inside the hair shaft. Homeopathic treatment here supports recovery; it does not replace them.

faqs.question: Is it contagious?
faqs.answer: The underlying fungal infection is. Combs, caps, towels and pillows should not be shared, and other children in the house are worth checking.

name: Head Lice
summary: Itchy scalp with nits cemented to the hair shafts — common, treatable and no reflection on hygiene.
intro: Head lice are extremely common among school-age children and spread by direct head-to-head contact. The itch comes from a reaction to louse saliva and often begins weeks after infestation. Repeated scratching is what turns a nuisance into a problem: broken skin invites bacterial infection, and prolonged inflammation can affect the hair. Treatment is mechanical and methodical, and every household member needs checking on the same day.
symptoms: Persistent itching, worst behind the ears and at the nape
Nits — pale oval eggs firmly cemented to the hair shaft near the scalp
Live lice visible on wet combing
Scratch marks, scabs or crusting on the scalp and neck
Disturbed sleep in children
Swollen glands at the back of the neck in longstanding cases
causes: Direct head-to-head contact, usually at school or during play
Shared combs, hair ties, caps, helmets and pillows
Incomplete treatment, allowing surviving eggs to hatch
Untreated household or classroom contacts leading to reinfestation
Long, untied hair increasing contact opportunity
treatment: Confirmation by wet combing with a fine nit comb — diagnosis by itch alone is unreliable
A structured combing schedule that covers the hatching cycle rather than a single session
Homeopathic prescription for the itch, scratched skin and any secondary infection
Simultaneous checking and, where needed, treatment of everyone in the household
Advice on shared items, and reassurance that this is not a hygiene failure

expectedResults.detail: Live lice numbers fall quickly with correct, repeated wet combing.
Completing the combing cycle clears newly hatched lice; itch settles as the reaction subsides.
Reinfestation is common where classroom contacts are untreated. Recurrence is not treatment failure — it is re-exposure.

faqs.question: Does this mean the hair is not being kept clean?
faqs.answer: No. Lice spread by head-to-head contact and are entirely indifferent to how often hair is washed. Clean hair is not protective, and infestation says nothing about hygiene.

faqs.question: Do I need to shave my child's head?
faqs.answer: No. Methodical wet combing over the full hatching cycle clears the infestation. Shaving is unnecessary and distressing for most children.

name: Pilar Cyst
summary: A smooth, firm, mobile lump under the scalp skin — usually harmless, occasionally inflamed, and definitively treated by removal.
intro: Pilar cysts, also called trichilemmal cysts, arise from the outer sheath of the hair follicle and occur on the scalp more than anywhere else. They are benign, often run in families, and frequently there is more than one. Most cause no trouble beyond being felt when combing. They become a problem when they enlarge, get knocked, become infected, or sit where a comb or helmet catches them. Definitive treatment is surgical removal of the cyst wall.
symptoms: A smooth, firm, round lump that moves with the skin over the skull
One or several lumps, often in family members too
Skin over the lump usually normal, sometimes stretched and thin-haired
Redness, pain and swelling if it becomes inflamed
A thick, pale, foul-smelling discharge if it ruptures
Catching on a comb, brush or helmet strap
causes: Proliferation of cells from the outer root sheath of a hair follicle
A clearly inherited tendency in many families
Local trauma to an existing cyst
Secondary bacterial infection after rupture
Repeated pressure or friction over the site
treatment: Examination to distinguish a straightforward pilar cyst from other scalp lumps
Homeopathic prescription for the tendency to recurrent cyst formation and for inflammatory episodes
Management of an acutely infected cyst, in coordination with medical care where antibiotics are needed
Referral for surgical excision where a cyst is large, recurrent, repeatedly inflamed or cosmetically troublesome
Prompt re-examination of any lump that changes in character, grows quickly or ulcerates

expectedResults.detail: Where a cyst is inflamed, the immediate aim is settling pain, redness and discharge.
Treatment is directed at reducing how often new cysts form and inflame.
An established cyst has a wall, and only removal of that wall clears it permanently. Medicine does not dissolve it — that expectation is set at the first consultation.

faqs.question: Can medicine make the lump disappear?
faqs.answer: Not an established cyst. It has a wall that continues to produce its contents, and only complete surgical removal of that wall resolves it. Treatment can help with inflammation and with the tendency to form new ones.

faqs.question: Is it cancer?
faqs.answer: Pilar cysts are benign. That said, any scalp lump that grows quickly, ulcerates, bleeds or changes character needs examining rather than assuming — which is why they are looked at rather than described over the phone.

name: Scalp Lichen Simplex Chronicus
summary: A thickened, leathery, intensely itchy patch of scalp maintained by an itch-scratch cycle that has become self-sustaining.
intro: Lichen simplex chronicus is the skin's response to being scratched and rubbed over a long period. On the scalp — most often at the nape or behind an ear — the skin thickens, its surface markings coarsen, and it itches more, which prompts more scratching. By the time it is seen, the original trigger may be long gone and the cycle itself is the disease. Breaking that cycle, including its stress and habit components, is the treatment.
symptoms: A well-defined, thickened, leathery patch, often at the nape or behind an ear
Intense itch, characteristically worse in the evening and at rest
Scratching that has become semi-automatic and unnoticed
Darkened or greyish discolouration of the affected skin
Broken hairs or thinning within the patch
Temporary relief immediately after scratching, followed by worse itch
causes: An original trigger such as eczema, an insect bite or a fungal patch
A self-sustaining itch-scratch-thicken cycle
Psychological stress, anxiety and habit
Heat, sweat and friction over the area
Contact irritation from hair products
Poor sleep, which lowers the itch threshold
treatment: Identification of the original trigger where one is still active
Constitutional homeopathic prescription, with weight given to the stress and habit dimension
Practical strategies to interrupt scratching, particularly at night
Review of hair products and anything applied to the area
Attention to sleep and anxiety, which reliably drive relapse

expectedResults.detail: Itch intensity is usually the first thing to change; scratching frequency follows.
As scratching reduces, the thickened skin gradually softens and normal surface texture returns.
Hair within the patch generally recovers once trauma stops. Relapse under stress is common, and is managed rather than treated as failure.

faqs.question: Why does it itch more at night?
faqs.answer: There is less to distract from the sensation, skin temperature rises, and for many people this is when the habit component is strongest. Managing the evening hours specifically is part of the plan.

faqs.question: Will the hair grow back in the patch?
faqs.answer: Usually yes. The hair loss here comes from breakage and repeated trauma rather than destruction of the follicle, so it recovers once the scratching stops.

name: Scalp Vitiligo & Poliosis
summary: Loss of pigment in a patch of scalp skin, with the hair growing white from it — a pigment condition, not a hair loss condition.
intro: Vitiligo on the scalp produces a pale, well-defined patch of skin, and the hair growing through it usually turns white — a change called poliosis. It is important to understand what this is and is not: the hair is not falling and the follicle is not damaged, it has simply stopped making pigment. Repigmenting scalp vitiligo, particularly once the hair has gone white, is difficult by any method, and this clinic is honest about that from the outset.
symptoms: A well-defined, milky-white patch of scalp skin
White hair growing from within that patch
A patch that is flat, not scaly, and not itchy
Sometimes a stripe of white hair at the front hairline
Depigmented patches elsewhere on the body in many patients
Increased tendency to sunburn over the affected skin
causes: Autoimmune destruction of pigment cells
Family history of vitiligo or other autoimmune disease
Associated thyroid disease, which is worth testing for
Physical trauma or injury at the site in some cases
Significant psychological stress preceding onset in some patients
treatment: Examination to confirm vitiligo rather than a scarring or fungal cause of a pale patch
Screening for associated autoimmune conditions, particularly thyroid disease
Constitutional homeopathic prescription directed at the autoimmune tendency and general health
Frank discussion of realistic expectations, including where repigmentation is unlikely
Referral to a dermatologist for phototherapy or surgical pigment transfer where that is the better option

expectedResults.detail: The first realistic aim is stability — no new or expanding patches.
Where repigmentation occurs it is slow and starts around follicles and patch edges.
Scalp patches with white hair repigment least readily, by any treatment. No one at this clinic will promise otherwise.

faqs.question: Will my hair colour come back?
faqs.answer: Often it does not. Repigmentation of hair in a vitiligo patch is the hardest result to achieve, because it needs pigment cells to repopulate the follicle itself. Skin repigmentation is more achievable than hair repigmentation.

faqs.question: Is my hair going to fall out?
faqs.answer: No. Vitiligo affects pigment, not the follicle's ability to grow hair. The hair grows normally — it simply grows white.

name: Hair Dye Allergy
summary: Allergic contact dermatitis to hair colourant — swelling, weeping and severe itch of the scalp, hairline and eyelids after dyeing.
intro: Hair dye allergy is usually a reaction to paraphenylenediamine (PPD) or a closely related compound. The pattern is characteristic: reaction begins hours to two days after application, and affects the scalp margins, ears, neck and eyelids more than the scalp itself. It is a true allergy, meaning it does not fade with repeated exposure — it intensifies. Occasionally reactions are severe enough to need emergency care, and everyone with this diagnosis should know the warning signs.
symptoms: Intense itching and burning of the scalp, hairline and ears
Redness, swelling and weeping, particularly of the eyelids and forehead
Onset several hours to two days after colouring, not immediately
Crusting and oozing in more severe reactions
Hair shedding for some weeks after a significant reaction
Progressively worse reactions with each subsequent exposure
causes: Paraphenylenediamine (PPD) and related dye intermediates
Black henna body art, a common route to becoming sensitised
Cross-reaction with certain azo dyes, sulphonamides and local anaesthetics
Continuing to dye after a mild first reaction
Skipping the patch test the manufacturer specifies
treatment: Confirming the reaction pattern and its timing, which is what distinguishes allergy from irritation
Homeopathic prescription for the acute dermatitis and the underlying allergic tendency
Clear written guidance on which products must now be avoided permanently
Discussion of alternatives, and of why 'natural' and 'PPD-free' labels cannot be taken at face value
Immediate referral to emergency care for facial swelling, breathing difficulty or extensive blistering

expectedResults.detail: Acute swelling, weeping and itch settle over roughly this period once exposure has stopped.
Skin texture and any post-reaction shedding recover as the scalp heals.
The sensitivity itself is lifelong. Treatment manages reactions and general allergic tendency; it does not make the dye safe to use again.

faqs.question: Can I use the dye again if I take treatment first?
faqs.answer: No. Contact allergy is not desensitised by treatment, and each exposure tends to produce a worse reaction than the last. Anyone telling you otherwise is putting you at risk.

faqs.question: Are herbal or natural dyes safe for me?
faqs.answer: Not automatically. Many products labelled natural still contain PPD, and 'black henna' is a frequent cause of sensitisation in the first place. Pure henna is a different substance, but the ingredient list — and a patch test — still matters.

name: Nevus Sebaceus
summary: A hairless, yellowish, slightly raised patch present on the scalp from birth or infancy, which changes in texture at puberty.
intro: Nevus sebaceus is a birthmark made up of sebaceous and follicular tissue. It appears as a smooth, hairless, yellow-orange oval patch, usually on the scalp or face, and is generally present from birth. It stays quiet through childhood, thickens and becomes more warty around puberty under hormonal influence, and carries a small risk of benign — and rarely malignant — growths developing within it in adult life. Because of that, it is monitored, and excision is sometimes advised.
symptoms: A hairless, oval or linear patch, usually yellow-orange, present from early life
A smooth surface in childhood that becomes thicker and bumpier at puberty
Absence of hair confined precisely to the patch
No itch or pain in the usual course
New nodules, bleeding or ulceration developing within it in adulthood — always a reason to be seen
causes: A congenital developmental anomaly of the sebaceous glands and follicles
A somatic genetic change occurring during development, not inherited from a parent
Hormonal stimulation at puberty, which drives the change in texture
Not caused by anything done during pregnancy or after birth
treatment: Confirmation of the diagnosis and baseline documentation of size and appearance
Homeopathic constitutional prescription for the child's or adult's general health
Structured monitoring, with photographs, for change in the lesion
Prompt dermatological or surgical referral if a nodule, ulcer or bleeding point develops
Discussion of elective excision, which is the only way to remove it, and its timing

expectedResults.detail: The realistic position is set out plainly: this is a structural birthmark, and no medicine removes it.
Monitoring at agreed intervals, with clear guidance on what changes warrant an earlier appointment.
Surgical removal is definitive and leaves a linear scar. Timing is usually a decision made with a dermatologist or plastic surgeon.

faqs.question: Will hair ever grow on it?
faqs.answer: No. The patch lacks normal hair follicles, and that will not change with treatment. Where it matters cosmetically, surgical excision is the option to discuss.

faqs.question: Is it dangerous?
faqs.answer: The great majority remain benign for life. There is a small, well-documented risk of tumours developing within it in adulthood, most of them benign — which is the reason for monitoring rather than for alarm.

name: Pseudofolliculitis Barbae
summary: Razor bumps — inflamed papules where shaved hairs curl back into the skin, most common and most stubborn in curly hair.
intro: Pseudofolliculitis barbae is not an infection. It is a foreign-body reaction to the person's own hair: a closely shaved curly hair re-enters the skin, either by curving back into the surface or by growing sideways inside the follicle, and the skin inflames around it. The beard area and neck are most affected. Shaving technique is central to both cause and cure, and no medicine substitutes for changing it.
symptoms: Small red or dark papules and pustules in the beard area and on the neck
Bumps appearing a day or two after shaving
Visible hair looping back into the skin within a papule
Itching, tenderness and occasional pus
Dark marks left behind long after the bump settles
Firm, keloidal scarring in longstanding cases
causes: Close shaving of tightly curled hair
Stretching the skin or shaving against the grain
Multi-blade razors cutting below the skin surface
Plucking, tweezing or picking at trapped hairs
An individual tendency to post-inflammatory pigmentation and keloid
Secondary bacterial infection of already inflamed papules
treatment: Examination to distinguish this from true bacterial folliculitis, which is managed differently
A specific, practical shaving protocol — this is the part that determines the outcome
Homeopathic prescription for the inflammatory tendency and the pigmentation that follows
Management of secondary infection where present
Referral for laser hair reduction discussion in severe or scarring cases, which is often the definitive answer

expectedResults.detail: New bump formation typically falls once shaving technique changes, often before any medicine takes effect.
Existing inflammation settles and the skin surface becomes smoother.
Dark marks fade over many months. Keloidal scars already formed do not resolve with medicine. Returning to close shaving reliably brings the condition back.

faqs.question: Will I have to grow a beard?
faqs.answer: Not necessarily, though letting the hair grow for a period is the fastest way to settle an acute flare. For most people the workable answer is a changed shaving method rather than stopping altogether.

faqs.question: Is laser hair removal worth considering?
faqs.answer: For severe or scarring cases, yes — it is the one approach that removes the cause rather than managing the effect. It is worth discussing with a dermatologist, and this clinic will say so plainly rather than keep you on treatment indefinitely.

name: Psoriasis
summary: Well-defined red plaques with silvery scale, driven by an immune process that speeds up skin turnover — chronic, relapsing and manageable.
intro: Psoriasis is an immune-mediated condition in which skin cells are produced far faster than they can be shed. The result is thickened, scaly plaques with sharply defined edges, most often on the elbows, knees, lower back and scalp. It runs a course of flares and quieter periods, and it is not contagious. Homeopathic treatment here is directed at the individual and the pattern of flares; nobody at this clinic will describe it as curable.
symptoms: Raised red plaques covered in silvery-white scale
Sharply defined edges, unlike eczema's blurred margins
Itching, and often a burning or tight sensation
Pinpoint bleeding if scale is scraped away
Nail pitting, ridging or separation from the nail bed
Joint pain and morning stiffness in a minority — this needs assessment
causes: Genetic predisposition, often with a family history
Immune activation driving accelerated skin cell turnover
Streptococcal throat infection, a classic trigger for guttate flares
Psychological stress
Skin injury, with plaques appearing along scratches or scars
Certain medications, smoking and alcohol
treatment: Assessment of pattern, extent and trigger history, plus screening questions for joint involvement
Constitutional homeopathic prescription — psoriasis responds to the person's whole picture, not to the plaques alone
Identification and management of individual flare triggers
Attention to stress, sleep and metabolic health, which measurably influence severity
Coordination with dermatology for extensive disease, and prompt referral if joints are involved

expectedResults.detail: Itch and the rate at which new plaques appear are usually what change first.
Existing plaques often thin and reduce in extent; flares tend to become shorter.
Psoriasis is a lifelong, relapsing condition. Realistic treatment aims at longer quiet periods and milder flares, not at permanent clearance.

faqs.question: Can psoriasis be cured?
faqs.answer: No — not by homeopathy and not by conventional medicine. It can often be controlled well enough that it stops dominating daily life, and that is the honest goal treatment is planned around.

faqs.question: Is it contagious?
faqs.answer: Not at all. Psoriasis cannot be passed to another person by touch, sharing a bed, a towel or a swimming pool.

faqs.question: Should I stop my dermatologist's treatment?
faqs.answer: No. Particularly with extensive disease or joint involvement, that treatment is doing important work. Treatment here is planned around it, not in place of it.

name: Eczema (Atopic Dermatitis)
summary: Dry, intensely itchy, inflamed skin with a defective barrier — often lifelong in tendency, usually controllable in practice.
intro: Atopic dermatitis is a barrier problem and an immune problem at once: the skin loses water and lets irritants in, and the immune system reacts to what gets through. It typically starts in childhood, often alongside asthma or allergic rhinitis, and follows a relapsing course. Scratching is not a side issue — it is the engine of the disease, and much of the treatment is about interrupting it.
symptoms: Dry, rough skin that itches persistently
Red, inflamed patches in the elbow and knee creases, neck, wrists and ankles
Weeping or crusting during flares
Thickened, leathery skin where scratching has been prolonged
Sleep disturbed by night-time itching
Frequent skin infections in the affected areas
causes: Inherited skin barrier defect, often with a family history of atopy
Immune sensitivity to environmental allergens
Soaps, detergents, wool and synthetic fabrics
Heat, sweat and sudden changes in climate
Dust mite exposure and, in some patients, specific foods
Stress and poor sleep, which worsen itch perception
treatment: Distinguishing atopic eczema from contact, seborrhoeic and fungal causes
Constitutional homeopathic prescription based on itch pattern, discharge, sleep and general disposition
A concrete barrier-care routine — moisturising is not optional in eczema, whatever else is prescribed
Identification of individual triggers rather than blanket food restriction, which harms children more often than it helps
Prompt treatment of secondary infection, and clear guidance on when topical steroids remain the right choice

expectedResults.detail: Itch intensity and sleep quality are usually the first meaningful changes.
Flares tend to become less frequent, and skin between them stays calmer.
The atopic tendency remains. Many children improve substantially with age; adults typically manage a condition rather than close the book on it.

faqs.question: Should I stop using steroid creams?
faqs.answer: Not on your own, and not during a significant flare. Used correctly for short periods, topical steroids control inflammation that would otherwise damage the skin further. Any plan to reduce them should be made deliberately, not abruptly.

faqs.question: Do I need to cut out foods?
faqs.answer: Only if a specific food genuinely and reproducibly triggers a flare. Broad elimination diets are common, rarely helpful, and in children risk real nutritional harm — so they are not advised without clear evidence.

name: Vitiligo
summary: Well-defined milky-white patches where pigment cells have been lost — a physically harmless condition with a heavy psychological weight.
intro: Vitiligo is an autoimmune loss of melanocytes, the cells that give skin its colour. Patches are flat, sharply defined and often symmetrical, favouring the face, hands, elbows, knees and areas around body openings. It causes no physical illness, but in India its social and emotional impact is substantial and treatment has to acknowledge that. Results vary enormously between patients, and honest expectation-setting is part of the first consultation.
symptoms: Flat, milky-white patches with clear borders
Frequently symmetrical distribution on both sides of the body
Common sites: around the mouth and eyes, hands, elbows, knees, genitals
White hair growing from within affected patches
Patches that sunburn readily
No itch, scale or pain in the usual course
causes: Autoimmune destruction of melanocytes
Family history of vitiligo or other autoimmune disease
Associated thyroid disease, diabetes or pernicious anaemia
Skin trauma, with new patches appearing at sites of injury
Significant emotional stress in a proportion of patients
Chemical exposure to certain phenolic compounds
treatment: Confirmation of diagnosis and mapping of every patch with photographs at baseline
Blood screening for associated autoimmune disease, particularly thyroid
Constitutional homeopathic prescription directed at the autoimmune tendency
Sun protection advice for depigmented skin, which burns easily
Honest discussion of phototherapy and surgical options, and referral where those are the better route

expectedResults.detail: The first aim is stability — halting the appearance and spread of new patches.
Where repigmentation happens, it appears as pigment islands around follicles and creeps in from the edges.
Response varies widely. Face and trunk repigment more readily; hands, feet, lips and patches with white hair often do not respond at all. This is stated at the outset, not after months of treatment.

faqs.question: How long before I see repigmentation?
faqs.answer: If it is going to happen, the earliest signs are typically several months in. Anyone offering a guaranteed timeline for vitiligo is not being straight with you.

faqs.question: Is it contagious or caused by eating the wrong foods?
faqs.answer: No on both counts. Vitiligo is autoimmune. It does not spread by touch, and no specific food combination — including the milk-and-fish belief common in India — causes it.

name: Acne
summary: Comedones, papules, pustules and nodules of the face, chest and back — treated with attention to scarring risk and hormonal drivers.
intro: Acne arises where excess sebum, blocked follicles, bacteria and inflammation meet. It is at its most common in adolescence but affects a substantial number of adults, particularly women, where it often signals a hormonal pattern worth investigating. Two things guide treatment here: how much inflammation is present, because that determines scarring risk, and what is driving it, because adult acne rarely responds to face washes alone.
symptoms: Blackheads and whiteheads on the forehead, nose and chin
Red papules and pustules, often tender
Deep, painful nodules or cysts in more severe cases
Oily skin with visible enlarged pores
Dark marks and pitted scars left after lesions heal
Flares timed to the menstrual cycle in many women
causes: Increased sebum production under androgen influence
Blockage of the follicular opening by retained keratin
Cutibacterium acnes overgrowth and the inflammation it provokes
PCOS and other hormonal patterns, particularly in adult women
Comedogenic cosmetics, hair oils and heavy sunscreens
Stress, sleep debt and, in some individuals, a high-glycaemic diet
treatment: Grading of severity and an explicit assessment of scarring risk
Investigation of hormonal drivers where the pattern suggests them, including PCOS
Constitutional homeopathic prescription reflecting the eruption pattern and general health
Review of skincare, cosmetics and hair products actually being used
Early referral where nodulocystic acne is scarring — delay here costs skin permanently

expectedResults.detail: Inflammation and tenderness in existing lesions usually settle before the overall count drops.
New lesion formation typically reduces; oiliness becomes more manageable.
Dark marks fade over six to twelve months. Pitted scars are permanent and need procedural treatment — no medicine fills them in.

faqs.question: Will treatment remove my acne scars?
faqs.answer: Dark marks fade with time and treatment. True pitted or ice-pick scars are structural and do not resolve with medicine — those need dermatological procedures, and you will be told so rather than kept on treatment expecting otherwise.

faqs.question: Does chocolate or oily food cause acne?
faqs.answer: The evidence for specific foods is weak and inconsistent, though high-glycaemic diets and, for some people, dairy do appear to worsen it. Diet is worth reviewing; it is rarely the whole story.

name: Urticaria (Hives)
summary: Itchy weals that appear and vanish within hours — acute after a trigger, or chronic and recurring for months with no clear cause.
intro: Urticaria produces raised, itchy weals from the release of histamine in the skin. The defining feature is that any individual weal lasts less than a day and leaves no mark. Acute cases usually follow an identifiable trigger. Chronic spontaneous urticaria — weals on most days for over six weeks — frequently has no identifiable trigger at all, which is frustrating but medically well recognised. Any episode with lip, tongue or throat swelling is an emergency.
symptoms: Raised, pale-centred weals with a red flare, of varying size
Intense itching, often worse in the evening
Individual weals resolving within 24 hours, leaving normal skin
New weals appearing elsewhere as old ones fade
Deeper swelling of lips, eyelids or hands (angioedema) in some patients
Weals induced by pressure, scratching, heat, cold or exercise in physical urticarias
causes: Foods, drugs — particularly NSAIDs and antibiotics — and insect stings in acute cases
Viral or parasitic infection
Autoimmune activity, which underlies a large share of chronic cases
Physical triggers: pressure, friction, cold, heat, sunlight, exercise
Associated thyroid autoimmunity
Stress, which does not cause it but reliably worsens it
treatment: A structured trigger history, and a symptom diary where the pattern is unclear
Screening for thyroid autoimmunity and other associations in chronic cases
Constitutional homeopathic prescription based on the character of the eruption and what modifies it
Realistic guidance on antihistamines, which remain the mainstay for acute control
Explicit emergency instructions for throat or tongue swelling or breathing difficulty

expectedResults.detail: In acute urticaria with an identified trigger, settling is usually rapid once exposure stops.
In chronic urticaria, the aim is fewer weal-free days becoming more weal-free days, and reduced reliance on antihistamines.
Chronic spontaneous urticaria often remits by itself over one to five years. Treatment aims to make that period liveable.

faqs.question: Why can't the cause be found?
faqs.answer: In chronic spontaneous urticaria, no external trigger is identified in the majority of patients — this is a documented feature of the condition, not a gap in the workup. Extensive allergy testing in these cases usually generates false leads rather than answers.

faqs.question: When is urticaria an emergency?
faqs.answer: Swelling of the lips, tongue or throat, difficulty breathing or swallowing, faintness or a rapidly spreading reaction. That is emergency care immediately — not a clinic appointment.

name: Fungal Skin Infection
summary: Ring-shaped, itchy, spreading patches of dermatophyte infection — extremely common in Kerala's humidity and increasingly resistant.
intro: Dermatophyte infection — tinea corporis, cruris and pedis — produces itchy, expanding patches with a raised, scaly edge and a clearer centre. Humidity, sweat and occlusive clothing make it very common here. Two things have changed the picture in India in recent years: widespread use of combination steroid-antifungal creams, which suppress the appearance while the infection spreads, and genuine antifungal resistance. Both are addressed directly rather than worked around.
symptoms: Itchy, ring-shaped patches with a raised, scaly, advancing border
Central clearing giving the classic ring appearance
Groin, inner thighs, waistband, underarms and feet most affected
Peeling and fissuring between the toes
Rapid spread to new sites and to household members
Altered, poorly defined appearance where steroid creams have been used
causes: Dermatophyte fungi thriving in heat and humidity
Prolonged sweating in tight or synthetic clothing
Sharing towels, clothes and bedding within a household
Over-the-counter steroid-antifungal combination creams, which worsen and disguise it
Diabetes and immunosuppression
Incomplete treatment courses, which drive resistance
treatment: Confirming it is fungal, particularly where steroid creams have altered the appearance
Immediate stopping of combination steroid creams, which are a major cause of treatment failure in India
Homeopathic prescription for the individual's susceptibility and recurrence pattern
Household-level measures: clothing, washing, drying and shared linen
Referral for oral antifungal therapy in extensive, resistant or recurrent infection — a common and appropriate need

expectedResults.detail: Itch and the spread of the advancing edge usually settle first.
Patches clear from the centre outwards; discolouration lingers after the infection has gone.
Recurrence is the rule where the household and clothing measures are not followed. Resistant infection needs oral antifungals, and you will be referred rather than kept waiting.

faqs.question: Why does it keep coming back?
faqs.answer: Usually one of three reasons: treatment stopped as soon as it looked better, other people in the house are infected and untreated, or a steroid-containing cream is being used. All three are addressed at the consultation.

faqs.question: Is the cream from the pharmacy safe to keep using?
faqs.answer: If it contains a steroid, no. Those combinations relieve itch quickly, allow the fungus to spread further and deeper, and have contributed directly to the resistant infections now seen across India.

name: Lichen Planus
summary: Violaceous, flat-topped, intensely itchy papules with a lace-like surface pattern, sometimes affecting the mouth, nails and scalp.
intro: Lichen planus is an inflammatory condition in which the immune system targets the basal layer of the skin. Its papules are distinctive: flat-topped, purplish, shiny, often crossed by fine white lines. It can involve the mouth, genitals, nails and scalp as well as the skin, and the scalp form is scarring — which makes early identification important. Most cutaneous cases settle within a year or two, leaving pigmentation behind.
symptoms: Flat-topped, purple-violet, shiny papules, typically on the wrists, forearms and ankles
Fine white lace-like lines over the papules (Wickham's striae)
Intense itch, often out of proportion to how the rash looks
White lacy patches or painful erosions inside the cheeks
Nail thinning, ridging or loss
New lesions appearing along a scratch line
causes: T-cell mediated autoimmune attack on basal skin cells
Association with hepatitis C in a proportion of patients, worth testing for
Drug-induced forms, from antihypertensives, antimalarials and others
Contact reaction to dental amalgam in oral lichen planus
Psychological stress as a recognised aggravating factor
treatment: Confirmation of diagnosis, with biopsy where the presentation is atypical
Screening for hepatitis C and review of current medications
Constitutional homeopathic prescription for the itch, the eruption pattern and the underlying tendency
Specific attention to scalp involvement, which scars, and to oral erosions, which need monitoring
Dermatological referral for erosive oral disease or rapidly progressive scalp involvement

expectedResults.detail: Itch is usually the first symptom to ease; new papule formation slows.
Existing papules flatten. Most skin lichen planus resolves within one to two years, with or without treatment.
Dark brown pigmentation persists for months to years after the papules go, and is not a sign of active disease. Scalp scarring and nail loss are permanent.

faqs.question: Will the dark marks left behind fade?
faqs.answer: Slowly. Post-inflammatory pigmentation in lichen planus is often deep and can take a year or more to lighten substantially. It is not active disease and does not mean treatment has failed.

faqs.question: Why do I need a hepatitis test?
faqs.answer: There is a well-documented association between lichen planus and hepatitis C. Testing takes one blood sample and occasionally uncovers something far more important than the rash.

name: Melasma
summary: Symmetrical brown patches across the cheeks, forehead and upper lip, driven by sun, hormones and heat — controllable, and prone to return.
intro: Melasma produces symmetrical patches of increased pigment on sun-exposed facial skin. It is far more common in women and in deeper skin types, and it is strongly linked to pregnancy, hormonal contraception and ultraviolet exposure. It is entirely harmless physically and often deeply distressing cosmetically. Sun protection is not an optional add-on to treatment — without it, nothing else works for long.
symptoms: Symmetrical light-to-dark brown patches on the cheeks, forehead, nose and upper lip
Irregular but well-defined borders
Darkening after sun exposure or a hot summer
Onset or worsening during pregnancy or on hormonal contraception
No itch, scale or discomfort
Partial fading in winter, returning the following season
causes: Ultraviolet and visible light exposure
Pregnancy and hormonal contraception
Genetic predisposition, particularly in deeper skin types
Heat itself, including cooking heat and hot climates
Thyroid dysfunction in a proportion of patients
Irritating cosmetics and, notably, previous use of skin-lightening creams containing steroids
treatment: Examination to establish whether the pigment is superficial, deep or mixed — this predicts how well it will respond
Thyroid assessment where the history suggests it
Constitutional homeopathic prescription addressing hormonal and general health factors
A rigorous, realistic sun protection plan including visible-light protection
Withdrawal of any steroid-containing fairness creams, which cause lasting damage

expectedResults.detail: The first realistic aim is stopping further darkening, which is largely about sun and heat exposure.
Gradual lightening, typically slow and uneven across the face.
Melasma recurs readily with sun exposure or a new pregnancy. It is managed long-term, not cleared once and forgotten.

faqs.question: How long will it take to clear completely?
faqs.answer: Complete and permanent clearance is not a promise anyone should make about melasma. Deep dermal pigment in particular responds poorly to every available treatment. Substantial lightening over months is a realistic aim.

faqs.question: Are fairness creams from the pharmacy safe?
faqs.answer: Many contain potent steroids and cause thinned skin, visible vessels and steroid-induced rosacea — and rebound pigmentation worse than the original. If you are using one, bring the tube to the consultation.

name: Warts
summary: Rough, raised growths caused by human papillomavirus — harmless, contagious to oneself and others, and often stubborn.
intro: Warts are benign growths driven by human papillomavirus infecting the top layer of skin. They spread by contact, including from one part of the body to another, and are especially common in children and in anyone whose skin is frequently wet or broken. Many resolve on their own over months to years as immunity develops. Treatment aims to hurry that along and to stop them spreading, and the response varies considerably between individuals.
symptoms: Rough, raised, skin-coloured growths with a cauliflower-like surface
Tiny black dots within the wart — thrombosed capillaries, not roots or seeds
Flat warts appearing in clusters on the face or backs of hands
Painful, inward-growing warts on the soles
Warts appearing in a line where skin has been scratched or shaved
Multiple warts spreading over weeks to months
causes: Human papillomavirus entering through minor breaks in the skin
Direct contact with another person's wart
Self-spread by scratching, picking, shaving or nail biting
Walking barefoot in shared wet areas
Reduced immunity from illness or medication
Damaged or macerated skin from prolonged wetness
treatment: Confirming these are viral warts and not corns, molluscum or something needing biopsy
Constitutional homeopathic prescription — warts are a classic indication where the individual's overall picture guides the remedy
Practical measures to stop self-spread: not picking, covering, footwear in shared wet areas
Attention to general immunity and any underlying illness
Referral for cryotherapy, cautery or excision where warts are painful, extensive or persistent

expectedResults.detail: The usual first sign is that no new warts are appearing.
Existing warts often soften, flatten and reduce, sometimes disappearing quite suddenly.

Response is genuinely variable — some clear quickly, some persist despite every approach. Where there is no meaningful change, procedural removal is discussed rather than treatment continued indefinitely.

faqs.question: Do warts have roots that must be removed?
faqs.answer: No. The black dots inside a wart are clotted blood vessels, not roots or seeds. Warts sit in the upper skin layers; nothing needs digging out.

faqs.question: Can they spread to my family?
faqs.answer: Yes, by direct contact and by shared towels, footwear and wet floors. Not sharing those items and keeping warts covered where practical are worth the effort.

name: Contact Dermatitis
summary: Red, itchy, sometimes blistering skin where something has touched it — irritant from repeated exposure, or allergic from true sensitisation.
intro: Contact dermatitis comes in two forms that look similar and behave differently. Irritant dermatitis is direct chemical damage — soaps, detergents, solvents — and affects anyone with enough exposure. Allergic contact dermatitis is an immune reaction in a sensitised person, appearing a day or two after contact with something most people tolerate. Telling them apart matters, because the first is about protection and the second about permanent avoidance.
symptoms: Redness, itching and burning confined to the area of contact
Small blisters, weeping and crusting in acute allergic reactions
Dryness, cracking and scaling in chronic irritant cases
A rash whose shape matches the object — a watch strap, a bindi, a footwear strap
Delayed onset, typically 24–72 hours, in allergic cases
Hands most commonly affected in occupational cases
causes: Detergents, soaps, cleaning agents and prolonged wet work
Nickel in jewellery, watch straps, buckles and spectacle frames
Cosmetics, fragrances and preservatives
Rubber and latex in gloves and footwear
Hair dye, henna and cosmetic adhesives
Plants, cement and occupational chemicals
treatment: Careful history mapping the rash's shape and timing against exposures
Distinguishing irritant from allergic contact dermatitis, which changes the advice entirely
Homeopathic prescription for the acute eruption and the underlying sensitivity
Specific, practical avoidance and barrier measures, including for occupational exposure
Referral for patch testing where the allergen cannot be identified from the history

expectedResults.detail: Once contact stops, acute redness, weeping and itch settle over roughly this period.
Chronic thickened, cracked skin — typically on hands — recovers more slowly and needs sustained barrier care.
In allergic contact dermatitis the sensitivity is permanent. Treatment manages episodes; avoidance prevents them.

faqs.question: Can I become un-allergic to nickel over time?
faqs.answer: No. Contact allergy generally persists for life. What changes is how well you avoid it — and coated or stainless alternatives usually make that practical.

faqs.question: Why is it worst on my hands?
faqs.answer: Hands do the contacting. Wet work, detergents and repeated washing strip the barrier, and once it is damaged, substances that were previously tolerated start to provoke a reaction.

name: Scabies
summary: Ferocious night-time itching from a burrowing mite — highly contagious, and never treated in one person alone.
intro: Scabies is an infestation by the mite Sarcoptes scabiei, which burrows into the top layer of skin. The itch is an allergic response to the mite and its products, which is why it can begin weeks after infestation and why it continues for a while after successful treatment. The distribution is characteristic: finger webs, wrists, waist, armpits, genitals. Everyone in the household is treated on the same day, symptoms or not — this is the single most common reason scabies persists.
symptoms: Severe itching, characteristically worst at night
Fine, wavy burrow lines in the finger webs and on the wrists
Small red papules around the waist, armpits, buttocks and genitals
Similar itching in other household members
Scratched, crusted or secondarily infected skin
In infants, involvement of the palms, soles and scalp, which is unusual in adults
causes: Prolonged skin-to-skin contact with an infested person
Shared bedding, clothing and towels
Crowded living or sleeping arrangements
Untreated household contacts causing reinfestation
Incomplete application of treatment, missing areas of the body
treatment: Clinical confirmation, looking specifically for burrows in the typical sites
Simultaneous treatment of every household member on the same day, whether itching or not
Homeopathic prescription for the itch, the scratched skin and any secondary infection
Precise instructions on scabicide application — head-to-toe, including under nails, and how long it stays on
Laundry and bedding protocol, with clear guidance on what actually needs washing

expectedResults.detail: The mites are killed by correctly applied treatment within the first application cycle.
Itching continues for two to four weeks afterwards as the allergic reaction settles. This is expected and does not mean treatment failed.
Persistent itching beyond four to six weeks, or new burrows, means reinfestation — usually from an untreated contact — and needs review.

faqs.question: Why am I still itching after treatment?
faqs.answer: The itch is an allergic reaction to mite proteins left in the skin, and it takes two to four weeks to settle after the mites are dead. Repeating scabicide treatment for this is common and unhelpful — it irritates the skin further.

faqs.question: Does everyone at home really need treating?
faqs.answer: Yes, on the same day, even those with no symptoms. Someone infested three weeks ago may not be itching yet, and they will reinfest the household as soon as your treatment finishes.

name: Rosacea
summary: Persistent central facial redness with flushing, visible vessels and acne-like bumps — trigger-driven, chronic, and readily aggravated by steroids.
intro: Rosacea affects the central face — cheeks, nose, chin and forehead — with flushing that becomes fixed redness over time, often with visible vessels and inflammatory papules. It is not acne, and treating it as acne with harsh regimens usually makes it worse. Individual triggers vary widely and identifying yours matters more than any general advice. Eye involvement is common and under-recognised, so it is specifically asked about.
symptoms: Easy flushing of the cheeks, nose and forehead
Persistent background redness that no longer fully settles
Fine visible blood vessels across the cheeks and nose
Red papules and pustules without blackheads — the distinction from acne
Stinging or burning when creams are applied
Gritty, dry, red eyes and recurrent styes
causes: Inherited vascular reactivity of facial skin
Sun exposure and heat
Spicy food, hot drinks and alcohol
Demodex mite density on facial skin
Topical steroids applied to the face, which cause a steroid-induced form
Emotional stress and sudden temperature change
treatment: Distinguishing rosacea from acne and from steroid-induced facial dermatitis
A personal trigger diary — the highest-yield step in most cases
Constitutional homeopathic prescription addressing the vascular reactivity and inflammatory component
A gentle skincare and daily sun protection routine; harsh actives are stopped
Withdrawal of facial steroids under supervision, and referral for ocular rosacea or rhinophyma

expectedResults.detail: Flushing frequency and papule formation usually respond before fixed redness does.
Background redness typically softens; skin becomes less reactive to products and weather.
Visible broken vessels do not resolve with medicine — laser is the effective option for those. Rosacea is a long-term condition managed through triggers.

faqs.question: Can I use my acne face wash on it?
faqs.answer: Usually not. Harsh cleansers, scrubs and strong actives aggravate rosacea's reactive skin. The routine is deliberately gentle, which is often the opposite of what people arrive doing.

faqs.question: I was given a steroid cream and it helped at first — why did it get worse?
faqs.answer: Facial steroids suppress redness briefly, then produce a rebound that is worse than the original condition. Coming off them takes a planned withdrawal, because stopping abruptly causes a severe flare.

name: Type 2 Diabetes
summary: Raised blood glucose managed alongside — never instead of — your physician's prescriptions and regular monitoring.
intro: Type 2 diabetes develops when the body's cells respond poorly to insulin and the pancreas cannot compensate. It is common, progressive if unmanaged, and mostly silent until complications appear. Homeopathic treatment at this clinic supports general wellbeing, energy, sleep and the many symptoms that accompany diabetes, including hair fall and skin problems. It does not replace metformin, insulin or any other prescribed medication, and no one here will suggest stopping them.
symptoms: Increased thirst and frequent urination, particularly at night
Fatigue that rest does not fix
Unexplained weight loss despite normal appetite
Slow-healing cuts and recurrent skin or urinary infections
Blurred vision that fluctuates
Numbness or tingling in the feet
Diffuse hair thinning and dry, itchy skin
causes: Insulin resistance, strongly linked to abdominal weight
Family history and genetic predisposition, marked in South Asian populations
Physical inactivity
Diets high in refined carbohydrate and sugar
Chronic stress and disturbed sleep
Previous gestational diabetes or PCOS
treatment: Review of your current HbA1c, fasting and post-meal glucose readings and existing prescriptions
Homeopathic prescription for associated symptoms, general vitality, sleep and stress
Practical, specific dietary and activity guidance suited to Kerala eating patterns
Attention to diabetes-related hair fall and skin problems, which are common and treatable
Coordination with — never replacement of — your treating physician, with periodic re-testing

expectedResults.detail: Energy, sleep, thirst and general symptom burden are the realistic early targets.
Where diet and activity changes hold, HbA1c often reflects them. Any medication change is your physician's decision, based on those numbers.
Diabetes is a lifelong condition needing continued monitoring, eye and foot checks. Treatment here is one part of that, not a substitute for it.

faqs.question: Can I stop my diabetes tablets?
faqs.answer: Not on the basis of homeopathic treatment. Glucose-lowering medication is prescribed against blood results, and only your treating physician should change it. Stopping without that is genuinely dangerous.

faqs.question: Can diabetes be reversed?
faqs.answer: Some people achieve sustained remission through substantial weight loss and dietary change, particularly early in the disease. That is a real phenomenon and worth pursuing — but it is a description of what diet and weight can do, not a promise attached to any medicine.

name: High Blood Pressure
summary: Persistently raised blood pressure — largely symptomless, seriously consequential, and managed alongside your physician's prescriptions.
intro: High blood pressure damages arteries, heart, kidneys, eyes and brain quietly over years, which is why it is measured rather than felt. Most people have no symptoms at all until something serious happens. Homeopathic treatment here supports the stress, sleep and general health factors that influence blood pressure. Antihypertensive medication, where prescribed, continues — the risk of stopping it is not theoretical.
symptoms: Usually none at all — this is the central point
Headache, particularly at the back of the head on waking, when very high
Dizziness or a feeling of unsteadiness
Palpitations or breathlessness on exertion
Visual disturbance in severe elevation
Nosebleeds occasionally, though far less often than commonly believed
causes: Family history and increasing age
Excess salt intake, which matters considerably in most Indian diets
Overweight and abdominal obesity
Physical inactivity
Chronic stress and poor sleep, including sleep apnoea
Alcohol, tobacco and certain medications
Underlying kidney or endocrine disease in a minority
treatment: Review of your home and clinic readings and current prescriptions
Homeopathic prescription addressing stress, sleep, headache and general constitution
Specific dietary guidance, with salt reduction addressed concretely rather than in general terms
Attention to weight, activity and alcohol
Coordination with your physician, and clear instruction on when a reading needs emergency care

expectedResults.detail: Symptom-level improvements — sleep, headache, stress tolerance — come first.
Where lifestyle changes hold, home readings often reflect them. Medication changes remain your physician's decision.
Hypertension usually needs lifelong management. Regular monitoring continues regardless of how well you feel.

faqs.question: Can I come off my blood pressure tablets?
faqs.answer: Only your prescribing physician can make that call, on the basis of sustained readings. Stopping antihypertensives on your own carries a real risk of stroke and heart attack, and this clinic will not advise it.

faqs.question: I feel fine — do I really need treatment?
faqs.answer: Yes. Hypertension is dangerous precisely because it causes no symptoms while it damages arteries. Feeling well is not evidence that the pressure is controlled.

name: Obesity & Weight Gain
summary: Excess body weight addressed as a metabolic and hormonal problem, not a failure of willpower — and without crash diets or false timelines.
intro: Weight gain is rarely just about eating too much. Thyroid function, insulin resistance, PCOS, medication, sleep debt, stress and previous crash dieting all shape it, and in South Asian bodies metabolic risk begins at a lower BMI than international charts suggest. Treatment here starts by finding what is actually driving it. There are no fixed-result packages and no promised kilograms per month at this clinic.
symptoms: Weight gain concentrated around the abdomen
Fatigue and breathlessness on modest exertion
Joint pain, particularly knees and lower back
Snoring and unrefreshing sleep
Excessive sweating and heat intolerance
Skin changes: darkened neck folds, chafing, fungal infection
Low mood and poor self-esteem, which both drive and follow the weight
causes: Energy intake persistently exceeding expenditure
Hypothyroidism, PCOS and insulin resistance
Medications including steroids, some antidepressants and antipsychotics
Sleep deprivation and shift work
Chronic stress and emotional eating
Repeated crash dieting, which lowers metabolic rate over time
Genetic and family patterns
treatment: Assessment for thyroid disease, PCOS and insulin resistance before anything else
Constitutional homeopathic prescription addressing appetite, cravings, energy and emotional eating
Realistic, sustainable dietary guidance built around Kerala foods rather than imported meal plans
Attention to sleep, stress and activity, which usually matter more than people expect
Referral where bariatric or specialist metabolic care is the more appropriate route

expectedResults.detail: Energy, appetite regulation and cravings are usually the first things to change.
Gradual, sustained weight change where the underlying driver has been identified and the changes are being kept up.
Weight regain is common when changes stop, whatever the method. No rate of loss is guaranteed here, and any clinic promising one should be treated with suspicion.

faqs.question: How many kilos will I lose in a month?
faqs.answer: That is not a number this clinic will give you. Rate of loss depends on the underlying cause, starting point, medication and what you sustain. Guaranteed-result weight loss packages are a marketing device, not medicine.

faqs.question: My thyroid is normal — why can't I lose weight?
faqs.answer: Insulin resistance, PCOS, sleep debt, medication effects and years of restrictive dieting all suppress weight loss with a normal thyroid. Which of these applies is what the first consultation is for.

name: High Cholesterol
summary: Abnormal blood lipids — a silent cardiovascular risk factor, managed with diet, activity and, where indicated, your physician's medication.
intro: Dyslipidaemia means an unfavourable balance of blood fats: raised LDL cholesterol, raised triglycerides, low HDL, or some combination. It produces no symptoms whatsoever, and its significance is entirely in the cardiovascular risk it carries over years. South Asians tend towards a particularly adverse pattern at lower body weights. Treatment here supports diet, weight and metabolic health, and works alongside statin therapy where that has been prescribed.
symptoms: None — dyslipidaemia is detected on a blood test, not felt
Fatty yellowish deposits around the eyelids in some patients
A pale ring around the cornea, particularly if it appears before middle age
Chest discomfort or breathlessness only when disease has already progressed
Frequently found alongside diabetes, hypertension or fatty liver
causes: Diets high in refined carbohydrate, sugar and fried food
Physical inactivity and abdominal obesity
Genetic patterns, including familial hypercholesterolaemia
Diabetes, hypothyroidism and kidney disease
Alcohol, which particularly raises triglycerides
Certain medications
treatment: Review of your lipid profile alongside overall cardiovascular risk, not the cholesterol number in isolation
Screening for hypothyroidism and diabetes, which commonly underlie abnormal lipids
Homeopathic prescription for general metabolic health, digestion and stress
Specific dietary guidance, with attention to coconut oil, fried snacks and refined carbohydrate as they feature locally
Coordination with your physician on statin therapy where cardiovascular risk warrants it

expectedResults.detail: Dietary and activity changes generally move triglycerides first — sometimes substantially.
Repeat lipid profile to assess objectively. LDL responds more slowly and less predictably to lifestyle alone.
Where risk is high or there is a strong family pattern, medication is often necessary regardless of lifestyle, and that is said plainly rather than avoided.

faqs.question: Can I stop my statin?
faqs.answer: That is a decision for the physician who prescribed it, based on your overall cardiovascular risk. In people with established heart disease or very high risk, stopping is a serious matter and this clinic will not encourage it.

faqs.question: Is coconut oil bad for cholesterol?
faqs.answer: Coconut oil raises LDL more than most vegetable oils — that much is consistent in the evidence. Quantity matters more than a ban, and the fried-food context it usually arrives in matters more still.

name: Fatty Liver Disease
summary: Fat accumulation in liver cells, usually found incidentally on a scan — largely reversible in its early stages through weight and diet.
intro: Non-alcoholic fatty liver disease is now extremely common, and most people discover it on an ultrasound done for something else. In its early grade it causes no symptoms and no damage. What matters is whether it progresses to inflammation and scarring, and the strongest determinant of that is body weight and metabolic health. This is one of the more genuinely reversible chronic conditions, and treatment reflects that.
symptoms: None in most cases — usually an incidental ultrasound finding
Vague fullness or discomfort in the right upper abdomen
Fatigue and a general sense of sluggishness
Bloating and poor digestion
Mildly raised liver enzymes on a blood test
Darkened skin at the neck folds, reflecting insulin resistance
causes: Insulin resistance and abdominal obesity
Type 2 diabetes and metabolic syndrome
High intake of sugar, particularly fructose, and refined carbohydrate
Physical inactivity
Rapid weight loss or crash dieting, which can paradoxically worsen it
Certain medications, and alcohol in the alcoholic form of the disease
treatment: Grading on ultrasound and review of liver enzymes and metabolic bloods
Screening for diabetes, thyroid disease and dyslipidaemia
Homeopathic prescription for digestion, appetite, energy and the metabolic picture
Focused dietary guidance on sugar, refined carbohydrate and portion size
A graded, sustainable weight loss plan — the intervention with the best evidence behind it

expectedResults.detail: Digestion, bloating and energy typically improve early.
A 7–10% reduction in body weight is where measurable improvement in liver fat usually appears. Repeat imaging and enzymes assess it objectively.
Established fibrosis or cirrhosis is a different matter, needs hepatology care, and does not reverse with diet. Grade determines what is realistic.

faqs.question: Is fatty liver serious?
faqs.answer: In its early grades, usually not — and it is largely reversible. It becomes serious if it progresses to inflammation and scarring, which is why weight and metabolic health are treated as the priority rather than the incidental finding itself.

faqs.question: I don't drink alcohol — how do I have fatty liver?
faqs.answer: Non-alcoholic fatty liver disease is driven by insulin resistance, abdominal weight and dietary sugar, not alcohol. It is now the commonest liver condition worldwide, in people who have never touched a drink.

name: Asthma
summary: Reversible airway narrowing with wheeze, cough and breathlessness — treated alongside inhalers, which are never stopped on our advice.
intro: Asthma is chronic airway inflammation with reversible narrowing, driven by triggers that differ from person to person. Homeopathic treatment here is directed at the underlying allergic tendency, frequency of episodes and general resilience. It is offered strictly alongside inhaler therapy. Reliever and preventer inhalers save lives in asthma; no one at this clinic will tell you to stop them, and anyone who does should be left behind.
symptoms: Wheezing, especially on breathing out
Breathlessness that comes in episodes
Cough that is worse at night and in the early morning
Chest tightness
Symptoms provoked by dust, cold air, exercise, smoke or infection
Waking at night from cough or breathlessness — a key marker of poor control
causes: Inherited allergic tendency, often with eczema or allergic rhinitis alongside
House dust mite, pollen, mould and animal dander
Respiratory infections
Cold air, humidity changes and the monsoon
Smoke, incense, mosquito coils and occupational dusts
Exercise, aspirin and NSAIDs in some patients
Emotional stress
treatment: Assessment of control: night waking, reliever use and effect on daily activity
Constitutional homeopathic prescription for the allergic tendency and episode frequency
Systematic trigger identification and practical household allergen measures
Clear instruction on correct inhaler technique, which is wrong more often than not
A written plan for what to do in an acute attack, and when to reach emergency care

expectedResults.detail: Night-time symptoms and reliever inhaler frequency are the practical measures used.
Many patients find episodes become less frequent and less severe over a season.
Any reduction in preventer inhaler dose is decided by your treating physician on the basis of sustained control — not by us, and not by how you feel on a good week.

faqs.question: Can I stop my inhalers?
faqs.answer: No, not on our advice. Preventer inhalers control the underlying inflammation, and stopping them is a common route to a severe attack. Dose reduction is a decision for your physician after a sustained period of good control.

faqs.question: Are inhalers habit-forming?
faqs.answer: No. This belief is widespread and causes real harm. Inhalers deliver medication directly to the airways at low dose — they are not addictive, and avoiding them leads to worse disease, not less.
